items.title: [Draft] EXL3 Flash Next on CUDA: TP=2, BF16 paging, cache reuse, graphs
items.body:
**Draft for upstream review; not merge-ready.** This ex3-on-upstream-wip/branch/exl3-on-upstream-wip integrates the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next EXL3 path with upstream `main` (base `d1018b318`). It is a broad working draft intended to be split into focused PRs before merge. The implementation has working paths, but required correctness, capacity, and performance gates remain open; in particular, CUDA graphs have not demonstrated a repeatable speedup. ## What it adds - EXL3 weight loading and CUDA execution in TensorFold's Flash Next path. - Routed-expert offload with per-layer GPU pools, pinned host banks, and asynchronous H2D staging. - Opt-in persistent decoder/MTP expert-frequency priors, with private per-model/rank storage, checked reload, adaptive startup decay, pool warming and atomic graceful-stop saves. - Expert-parallel TP=2 with split routed experts, shared-expert execution, vocabulary-sharded `lm_head`, and NCCL collectives. - BF16 KV paging to host RAM, snapshots/restores, and prefix/cache reuse, with an opt-in per-rank shared block arena. Ordinary-context private/shared snapshot and served reuse gates pass; the 200k × 2 target remains unqualified. - MTP drafting and CUDA graph capture/replay. Decode graphs cover eligible rounds/windows; prefill graphs capture dense sub-blocks, while expert scheduling/copies remain eager. These are implemented paths in the branch, not claims that every supported shape or failure mode is validated. The evidence and remaining gates below define what has actually been checked. ## Memory and execution split Configuration shown: **TP=2 with BF16 KV paging enabled** (`TF_FLASHNEXT_KVPAGE=1`). Each request uses both GPUs. The boxes show placement, not allocation sizes. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph HOST["CPU scheduling and host RAM"] direction TB RAM0["Rank 0 RAM

MoE all-reduce
Logit all-gather"] GPU1 <--> NCCL classDef gpu fill:#e8f2ff,stroke:#3765a3,color:#152b46 class GPU0,GPU1 gpu ``` - **Replication and sharding:** paging currently disables attention-head sharding, so each rank has the full attention/KV layout and its own host backing allocation. Decoder routed experts and `lm_head` vocabulary columns remain split. With paging disabled, a separate attention-head split is available; it is not the configuration drawn here. - **Expert movement:** host-planned paths use asynchronous H2D copies. The deep-prefill ring reuses decoder pool storage across layers. In device-planned decode, GPU kernels read mapped host banks to fill cache lines; overflow experts can be read in place. Routed caches retain experts for reuse, while the shared expert has a separate resident allocation on rank 1. CPU scheduling does not mean CPU expert execution. - **KV and snapshots:** selected older KV blocks are fetched into the device block cache; recent window rows are written back to RAM during window rebasing or snapshot flushing. Snapshots preserve host KV history, device windows/cache contents, pager tables, and recurrent/PLE/MTP state where present. The PLE table itself is file-backed; gathered embeddings are uploaded. - **Shared block option:** `TF_FLASHNEXT_KVPAGE_SHARED=1` uses one block pool per rank with fixed per-lane windows and generation-tagged ownership. Private per-sequence paging remains the default. Shared version-2 snapshots retain only owned blocks and remap them into destination slots; they do not overwrite the whole arena or deduplicate identical-prefix payloads. Capacity pooling can trade cache hits for VRAM, so it is not a throughput claim. - **Scope:** the NCCL box denotes logical communication, not a direct GPU peer link. Memory budgets depend on configuration. Ordinary-context TP=2 paging/cache behavior has been exercised; 200k × 2 with paged KV remains unproven. Prefill expert scheduling/copies remain eager when dense prefill graphs are enabled. ## Proposed PR segmentation This is a proposed split plan, not a claim that the listed PRs already exist. Each future PR should own one coherent layer, add focused tests, and record its correctness and performance evidence. Until then, this mega PR remains a tracking draft and should not be merged as one piece. The current branch already contains prototype implementations for these areas; the listed gates are remaining review/acceptance criteria. 1. **EXL3 foundation and resident forward:** isolate format/config parsing, weight loading, and the upstream CUDA adapter. Acceptance: layer/model oracle gates for the resident path. 2. **Expert pool and offload:** isolate host-bank layout, device line pools, replacement policy, async copies, and pool lifecycle. Acceptance: pooled output matches resident execution; measure copy/compute overlap rather than assuming it. 3. **TP=2 execution and serving:** isolate expert partitioning, shared-expert placement, vocabulary-head split, collectives, and rank lifecycle. Acceptance: TP=2 logits/outputs meet a defined numerical tolerance and the server works on both GPUs. 4. **BF16 KV paging and state reuse:** isolate device/host page tables, paging/eviction, paged snapshots/restores, and prefix branching. Acceptance: paged/resident equivalence where comparable; exact state/logit parity for snapshot/restore and cache reuse, plus long-context tests. 5. **MTP drafting:** isolate draft-head input, TP=2 draft/verify, and prompt-cache interaction. Acceptance: committed drafted tokens equal serial decoding with drafting disabled. 6. **CUDA graph decode:** isolate stable graph inputs/outputs, TP=2 collectives, offload boundaries, and capture/replay lifecycle. Acceptance: graph/eager output equality over repeated replay and snapshot restore. 7. **CUDA graph prefill and scheduling:** isolate chunked capture, expert-major scheduling, staging overlap, and profiling-driven tuning. Acceptance: repeatable graph-on improvement in controlled prefill/decode measurements without correctness or memory regressions. 8. **Final capacity and product integration:** run repeated 200k-context × 2-concurrency TP=2 tests with BF16 paging/cache reuse, resource margin, and failure cleanup; then consider family/recipe registration. Do not register until preceding gates pass. Proposed dependencies: the foundation precedes the other slices; expert offload and TP=2 build on it; paging needs stable TP=2 allocation/lifecycle; MTP needs TP=2 and cache semantics; graph work depends on stable paging/offload and eager behavior. Decode and prefill graph slices can be developed in parallel once interfaces are fixed, but should be integrated and reviewed in dependency order. Avoid duplicate implementations: use stacked branches or clean cherry-picks, and keep this umbrella draft as an index until the sequence is complete. ## Benchmark report The detailed tables, exact tested commit, model/checkpoint identity, runtime configuration and methodology are in the [21 October benchmark comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6315696853). These historical results apply to source `ca2b13c88315c9c1c7a9ce17c002226f3585f73a`, not subsequent candidate changes. The single matched graph/eager run did not establish a speedup. ## Evidence and remaining gates - **Prior replay/cache correctness checkpoint:** runtime `4afc6169` passes 192 EXL3 host tests, real native/GPU-runner builds, private/shared buffer-reuse/snapshot checks on both cards, and exact TP2 prefill origin/grid rebinding through dense/sparse and paging-split transitions. The native MTP/graph/shared-BF16 cold/warm/branch/rewind gate retains all eight reference hashes. [Exact sources, binaries, model, methodology and scope](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792). Correctness-run timings overlapping compilation are excluded; isolated graph speedup remains unproven. Retaining buffers does not retain old-owner graphs. - **Prior replay/cache telemetry checkpoint:** runtime `975c1df9` passes 177 EXL3 host tests, the native CUDA build, diagnostics-enabled TP2 shared-BF16 cache reuse with separate valid expert/KV counters, and diagnostics-disabled c8 hash/replay qualification. Source `b3a7b565` also passes the focused real TP2 width-3/4/16 rebind fixture. [Full source, model, methodology and bounded measurements](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6327563987). Those receipts do not qualify subsequent runtime changes. No repeatable speedup, independent golden fidelity or 200k capacity is inferred. - **New shared BF16 checkpoint:** historical runtime [`ccb32fc3`](https://github.com/BlivionIaG/TensorFold/commit/ccb32fc3ba313bbde74401e305f572234c9bbe81); these direct fixture results are not relabeled as current-head tests. 153 EXL3 host tests and real native/GPU-test CUDA builds pass. Matched TP=2 private/shared sparse-paging fixtures pass exact restored-state checks, owned-entry remapping, recycled/asymmetric generations, foreign-request isolation and actual prefill/decode graph replay. Two 16,424-token HTTP histories with MTP and graphs pass cold/warm/branch/rewind reuse against the private reference. The [full qualification comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6325790752) separates these tests from the earlier same-binary `0de41d37` allocation measurement (920 MiB lower sampled peaks per GPU). Shared mode stays opt-in; none of these results establishes independent model fidelity, repeatable graph speedup or 200k × 2 capacity. - **Served BF16 paging/cache gate on `ca2b13c8`:** two concurrent HTTP histories, each with 16,424 prompt tokens and 32 generated tokens, passed cold, warm, branch and rewind phases with graphs and MTP enabled. Full response hashes matched a separately started cache-disabled reference for every phase. Cache-enabled requests reused 16,407–16,417 tokens on warm/branch/rewind phases; warm native prefill times were 0.944 / 0.974 seconds. This proves ordinary-length prefix reuse and continuation parity, not long-context capacity, independent model fidelity, or exact internal-state parity at this new head. - **Completed matched graph/eager gate on `ca2b13c8`:** all four exact 1024/512 and 16384/1024 cases at c1/c8 passed in each mode (36 valid responses, 18/18 matching full token/text hashes). Binary and per-rank expert geometry were identical. Both ranks replayed decoder graphs while all eight requests decoded in each c8 cell, and replayed prefill graphs in the long-input cells. Graph-run physical GPU peaks were 14,958 / 14,996 MiB; automatic expert pools were 10 / 23 lines per layer. This is an ordinary-context functional/capacity pass, not a 200k claim. - **21 October checkpoint:** source `ca2b13c8` is integrated without rewriting the draft history. The parent EXL3 host gate passes 90/90 tests, scoped formatting/diff checks pass, all tracked source hashes match the Linux build tree, and the native CUDA sm_120 build succeeds. This adds workload-scaled graph budgets, class-aware local graph charges, selective coordinated TP LRU retirement, and a tested local-reclamation fallback. Graph memory charges remain heuristic, not measured exec sizes. - **New snapshot hardware receipt:** on the preceding `d3662d1b` runtime with test-only upstream loader compatibility fixes, both RTX 5060 Ti ranks passed the compiled two-lane BF16-paged snapshot fixture. Restored canonical KV history, recurrent/index/PLE state and continuation logits matched exactly. Each graph iteration recorded 27 prefill and 5 decode replays per rank. This uses 24 expert lines per layer and no MTP head; it is not an eight-lane capacity, served prefix-cache, or 200k test. The new checkpoint separately passes the served cache-reuse gate below; this older direct state/logit fixture is not relabeled as a current-tree run. - **Performance remains an acceptance blocker:** graph decode was 3.4–5.4% slower across the four cells in this single matched pair. No repeatable speedup is established. Cache-key churn and the graph/expert/KV memory partition remain optimization work; increasing reserved memory is not itself a performance fix. The earlier interrupted diagnostic overlapped compilation and is not a controlled performance receipt. - On earlier source-tree revisions, TP=2 serving, draft-on/off output parity, BF16 paging, snapshot/cache reuse, and graph/eager correctness were exercised on development hardware. These results are not a full validation of the exact current PR head. - CUDA graphs currently match eager in tested paths, but controlled profiling has not established a graph-on speedup. That is a hard performance gate, not a claimed win. - The strict golden-prompt near-tie and remaining TP numerical-parity questions still require closure. - Ordinary-context TP=2 private/shared paging, scoped state/logit restoration, graph replay and served cache reuse now pass on runtime `ccb32fc3` as described in the qualification comment. Cancellation/overflow/live-rank failure injection, repeated performance qualification and the 200k × 2 BF16 paging target remain required before merge/registration. The earlier near-200k × 2 retrieval test used resident BF16 KV and is not evidence for paged-KV capacity. - Fresh `tools/zig/lean_check.py` run: 1,762 findings on the current source versus 444 on pinned upstream `d1018b318` (1,318 more). This remains a CONTRIBUTING blocker, not a clean result. - CPU expert execution is out of scope. BF16 remains the required KV-cache format; int8 KV is not part of the serving path. Branch: `exl3-on-upstream-wip` Current fork head: `0272aafe266299c078976c74fbe5347bdf484f7c` (qualified target-layer history, DMA coalescing, opt-in transfer provenance and actual-layer GDN graph keys; bounded TP2 BF16 cache/parity and screening measurements pass) Upstream base: `d1018b318fb51981c4a18f12e40269a4d3ee9713` ### Persistent expert-profile checkpoint (22 October) Native source `babc9762e2dbc999c9b68df252d619830203d693`, binary SHA-256 `86a7b20b6bac2bc5b2b78f9c89654a21cd1c0bd2ad9e6806ee1dc70abe110907`, passes a real TP2 graceful stop/start gate with graphs, MTP and shared BF16 paging: two waves of two concurrent 1,024-input/64-output requests in each fresh process pair, prefix cache off, fixed pools 32/48. Both ranks save, reload, warm and update their profiles; response hashes match across restart. The leader is signalled and the existing TP stop protocol releases the follower. Startup warms 1,568 / 2,304 existing lines, with no pool enlargement. The profile checkpoint also passes 211 host tests and 15 focused Linux Debug/ReleaseSafe persistence tests; a separate source-53ef CUDA fixture verifies actual bytes/tables and resized pool restart on both GPUs. Enable with `TF_FLASHNEXT_EXL3_PROFILE_DIR`. The advisory fingerprint covers routed trellis plus config/index bytes, not every checkpoint tensor; hashing costs about 16.6 seconds per rank at startup in this gate. Counts are decayed once and saved by replacement, not added twice. The separate deep-prefill ring histogram is not persisted; prefill may discard startup residency. Abrupt follower/process kills can lose unsaved updates. These are placement priors, not KV snapshots or elastic budgeting. A separate short-prompt ABBA with drafts off measured 9.0% lower TTFT and 6.5% lower decode latency for warm versus cold persisted profiles (TP=2, graphs and BF16 paging on; 128-token input / 64-token greedy output; identical full output hashes). This narrow result is not evidence for long-context or drafted-serving gains, nor a graph speedup; profile fingerprinting adds about 16.6 seconds of startup per rank. Full methodology and values are in the [final report](https://github.com/BlivionIaG/TensorFold/blob/exl3-on-upstream-wip/docs/plans/exl3-on-upstream-final-report.md). No independent golden-fidelity, long-prefill-speed or 200k×2 gate is closed by this test. ### Latest prefill efficiency candidate `ce10271d` starts initial expert copies before CPU member-list construction and coalesces copy-stream dependencies for equal/older release epochs, preserving newer-reader and event-wrap guards. It passes 215 EXL3 host tests, native CUDA host/forward-body compilation, formatting/diff checks and zero new lean findings. **Native TP2 BF16 cold/warm/branch/rewind parity now passes for the specified ce10271d workload; the matched ce/babc revision comparison is effectively flat. Independent model fidelity and 200k capacity are not inferred.** Previous hardware receipts apply only to their named sources. Copy-grid-only tuning (144/36/36/144, frozen native `babc9762`, TP2 c2, 1k/256, two waves/server) was 0.3–0.5% slower in both ordered pairs with exact response parity; the default stays unchanged. ### Latest measured follow-up `a25fa226` passes a real native TP2 gate with two concurrent 16,424-token histories, MTP, prefill/decode graph replay, BF16 RAM paging and prefix reuse at 4096-row prefill. All eight cold/warm/branch/rewind outputs match the separate cold reference. Demand/initial-prefetch/cross-layer-prefetch copy and requested-byte categories reconcile on both ranks. Native SHA256: `939f5ef182c9bfefb1efe2a3847715c32011b734f703427a52a311ada61df5bf`; 222 EXL3 +218 runtime host tests pass, zero new lean findings. The previous `ce10271d` revision showed no meaningful speedup against its baseline. Profiling identified expert-transfer volume and many separate projection DMA submissions. The new direct-copy helper combines projections only with proven common pinned-bank provenance and exact adjacency, with guarded fallback; no CUDA arithmetic or graph ownership checks were weakened. The matched ce/a25 code comparison at identical4096-row settings is complete and shows no repeatable gain; one pair has worse decode/ITL. A subsequent matching-target-layer-history candidate passes native cache parity and all16 benchmark hashes/replay checks in four fresh A/B/B/A servers, with about2.1% aggregate decode-service improvement in both screening pairs and only0.2–0.3% effective-prefill improvement. It is integrated with unchanged mandatory loading and graph/BF16-paging guards;227 host tests and native compilation pass. Two pairs do not establish statistical significance or causal graph/eager speedup; diagnostic total transfer volume is effectively unchanged. Tested source and binary, exact ratios and the separate current-default CUDA profile are recorded in the linked measurement comment. A separate four-fresh-server setting comparison shows 4096 versus forced2048 rows improves TTFT about39% and effective aggregate-prefill about64% on the stated TP2/c2 workload, with exact hashes and actual graph reuse. **4096 is already the engine default; the inherited benchmark harness forced2048. This is a setting comparison, not a new-code gain.** The8192 pilot is not accepted because cached-prefill replay failed its unchanged gate. Cross-request graph retention remains disabled pending complete captured-allocation lifetime proof. Full methodology, exact tested commits, units and limits are in the [existing measurement comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792). ### Dense EXL3 prompt-kernel update (22 October; pushed head `5a94359c07c8f716255ff9b0de7a7257dec1432f`) A Blackwell sm120+ mul1/C2 `ldmatrix.x4` input-fragment path is now included. The four fresh-server A/B/B/A TP2 screening pairs with 16,384 input / 256 output, c2, graphs/MTP, BF16 RAM paging, 4096-row prefill and pools 32/48 show effective aggregate-prefill +2.27%/+2.23% and TTFT −2.28%/−2.24%; aggregate decode-service +0.77%/+1.23%. All response hashes match. This is a small two-pair screening result, not statistical significance or graph/eager causality. The canonical candidate passes the BF16 paging/cache cold/warm/branch/rewind gate (8/8 responses) and changed-kernel CUDA/resource checks. Full kernel-contract timed out at 300 seconds on both GPUs; broad contract pass is not claimed. Exact methods, hashes, limits and assessment of the reviewer’s cache/page-table pointers are in the latest [measurement comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792).

items.title: qwen CUDA: long-prompt prefill 5.4x faster (4096-row chunks, tensor-core attention, the delta-rule chain)
items.body:
**Builds on #1079** (its nineteen commits come first here); the last two commits are this PR's.

Long-prompt prefill for the Qwen3.5 CUDA family. Measured on one RTX 5090 (Qwen3.8-27B MLX 4-bit + DFlash2, `--kv-cache fp8`, a 262,144-token window): a 75,616-token prompt took 144.5 s to its first token on main and takes 26.9 s here (56,143 tokens: 18.6 s).

A prompt pass ran in 128-row chunks: each projection's GEMM launched about 80 blocks on a 170-SM GPU, attention ran the decode kernel's one-warp-a-row partials, and the delta rule stepped through rows one warp a value row. Nsight's split for the 75,616-token prompt: attention 83 s, projections 56 s, the delta rule 3.4 s.

| Step | First token at 75,616 tokens |
|---|---|
| main | 144.5 s |
| tensor-core prompt attention (128-row chunks) | 108.7 s |
| 1024-row chunks | 38.0 s |
| 4096-row chunks | 32.9 s |
| v0.6.6's delta-rule chain | 29.2 s |
| the 2x2-warp prompt tile | 26.9 s |

**Kernels**
- `prefill_attention_rows.cuh` takes e4m3 cache rows with an fp32 scale each (`F8`: staged a step ahead and widened to bf16 in the slot) and head-major caches (`HM`: each key head's `CAP` rows in a run). `hpattn_kernel` and `hpattn8_kernel` instantiate them at head dim 256. `pattn_kernel`, `tree_kernel`, `full_kernel` and `vision_kernel` compile to identical SASS on sm_120.
- `gdn_prefill.cu`: v0.6.6's prompt chain for the gated delta rule (two threads a value row, 32 steps staged), β bf16 or fp32.
- `qmm_prefill.cu` adds the prompt tile on 2x2 warps and two stages; `Affine4Kernels.half_prompt` picks it (off by default; the Qwen3.5 engine sets it except on a GB10).

**Engine**
- A prompt chunk is up to 4096 rows (`Round.max_rows`, the tables' and activations' rows; the snapshot grid and cold-cut rule follow, so cache-on and cache-off passes still cut at the same rows). Verify windows stay within `most_verify`, and the decode partials are sized for those rows only. About 0.6 GiB more scratch on the 27B; a 262,144-token window still fits one stream on 32 GB.
- A one-part prompt chunk's attention runs `hpattn(8)_kernel` over the stream's own cache, and its delta rule `gdn_prefill`'s chain, from pointers the host reads off the staged segment (prompt passes are not captured).
- The drafters absorb a chunk's taps in pieces of `most_verify` rows, so their scratch does not grow with the chunk.

**Numerics.** Prompt arithmetic changes with the kernels, so greedy replies differ from main's where its rounding decides a token (on a 24-prompt mix, 10 of 24 replies are byte-identical to main's; the earlier qwen27 CUDA engine matches main on 11 of 24 with the same kernels). Decode rounds cost the same (16.13 to 16.20 ms). A needle at 40% of a 60,000-token prompt is found; greedy replies at 75,616 tokens are identical across fresh servers.

Checks: `zig build test`, `test-kernel-contract`, `test-golden`, `fuzz-cortheon`, the Flash Next gate test, `zig fmt` and the lean check pass, as do the `test-qwen35-*` host steps (the cold-cut test is now written in terms of `max_rows`).

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: the prompt DeltaNet block in one kernel a value head
items.body:
A lone stream's prompt pass runs the GDN block as three launches: `fn_gdn_front` writes every row's q, k, v, g and beta as fp32 (41 KB a row, 63 MB for a 1,536-row chunk), `fn_gdn_chain_tpr` reads them back for the delta rule, and `fn_gdn_norm` reads the fp32 readouts again for the gated norm. On a GB10 the front is bound by DRAM (~240 GB/s), so overlapping it with the chain on a second stream hides almost nothing (measured: -0.5 % at 1,536 rows).

`fn_gdn_fused` keeps those rows in shared memory:
- 256 threads walk the chain with `fn_gdn_chain_tpr`'s code;
- 128 producer threads make the next 16 rows' inputs with `fn_gdn_front`'s op sequence;
- the same producers run the gated norm of the previous 16 rows with `fn_gdn_norm`'s.

Every row's arithmetic is unchanged, so the bits are too. The recurrence is row by row, so where the rows are cut (chunk size, resume point) does not change them either. Passes of 64 rows or more on one stream use it; `TF_FLASHNEXT_GDN_FUSED=0` keeps the three launches.

| GDN block, GB10 | three launches | fused |
|---|---|---|
| 1,024 rows | 1.277 ms | 1.040 ms |
| 1,536 rows | 1.907 ms | 1.547 ms |
| 4,096 rows | 5.008 ms | 4.078 ms |

Bytes (state, readouts, gated rows, sums) are equal from 64 to 4,096 rows.

**Checks**
- Kernel contract: nonfinite, repeat and 6 shapes bit-equal to front -> rows_to -> norm. The gate-5 record covers sm_80/86/89/120/121 (nvcc 13.0.88; no 13.2/13.3 override).
- Full `zig build test -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`: exit 0 (278/278 steps; 3,491 of 3,506 tests passed, 15 skipped). lean_check: 0 new against the merge base. `zig fmt` is clean.

**Served Flash Next FP4-Local (MTP and prompt cache on, chunk 1,536)**

Token hashes: 136 of 136 equal to main's. This covers greedy and seeded, c=1 and c=4, and cold, warm and resumed requests.

| cold TTFT | main | fused |
|---|---|---|
| ~10k tokens | 7.81 / 7.85 s | 7.72 / 7.67 s |
| ~38k tokens | 30.98 / 30.24 s | 30.02 / 29.93 s |

That is about -1.5 to -2 %.

## Gotchas

- Branch `fn-gdn-fused` @ `c184e94c` (two commits), based on `main` @ `da275a360`; it test-merges cleanly onto today's `main` (`1705bf542`).
- It touches `cuda_batch.zig` and `cuda_batch_state.zig`, which #1113, #1069 and #896 also change, and `contract_tests.zig`, as #958, #982, #987 and #1141 do. These are textual conflicts only (the fused path is one branch in the GDN block's launch).
- The gate-5 record was made with nvcc 13.0.88 only; there's no 13.2/13.3 compiler on this machine.
- Batched (multi-stream) prompt passes and passes under 64 rows keep the three launches. The 27B (`qwen3_5` CUDA) is unchanged: there, every fused form I tried was exact but slower (its prepare step is compute-heavy and four producer warps can't keep up).

items.title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Metal: routed experts in the 27B's engine (slice 1 of #931)
items.body:
## What this changes

`qwen3_5_moe` checkpoints (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) serve text on the native Metal engine through the 27B's engine,
whose layers they share: each layer's MLP is now a tagged union of the 27B's dense MLP or routed experts. Slice 1
of #931. Images (slice 2) and MTP drafts (slice 3) are refused until their slices land.

- Routing is #856's rule: fp32 router logits, top-k by logit with ties to the lower id, weights
  `exp(l - l_top)` over the k rounded to bf16, the shared expert as one more slot weighted
  `bf16(sigmoid(bf16(gate)))`, the slots' weighted sum rounded once to bf16. The logits run on
  `core/moe_route`'s kernel; selection, the by-expert sort and the weighted sum are three new kernels in
  `kernels/metal/qwen27/moe.metal`; the experts run on `core/tile_qmm`'s prompt tiles and decode twin.
- The places that pinned the 27B's shape read the config: attention's head counts (the kernels take
  `Q27_GROUP`/`Q27_KV_HEADS` defines whose defaults are the 27B's 6 and 4, so the 27B compiles without them),
  the K/V unpack width, the cache size check and the shape check.
- `core/moe_route.metal`: a logits lane stops at the row's end. Each lane took four 32-wide steps, which assumed
  GLM's 4,096; at 2,048 the last lanes read past the router's rows. At 4,096 the guard is never taken.
- Prompt cache and `--parallel` lanes come with the 27B's host, so they are qualified here (their receipts
  below), and #931's slice 3 folds into this one.
- Widths, on Metal only: MLX affine 4-bit experts in groups of 64 with 8-bit routers; other expert widths are
  refused at load (8-bit experts are slice 4). `--drafter`, `--vision` and image parts are refused.
- qwen27's saved-state identity hashes its kernel sources, so the 27B's saved conversation states from an older
  build are not reused after this change.
- The 35B's config, expert loader and adapter are the Qwen3.5 family's (`families/qwen3_5/config.zig`,
  `metal_experts.zig`, `metal_native_moe.zig`): qwen27 reads config.json through the family reader for the dense
  27B and the 35B alike, and the experts load in the 27B's one layer loop. The reader no longer crashes on zero
  heads or `mrope_section` values near the 64-bit limit; it returns its ordinary errors.

## Design: one engine, and the alternatives

The 35B is the 27B's architecture (Gated DeltaNet layers, gated full attention every fourth layer) at smaller
sizes with routed experts in place of the dense MLP, so it runs the 27B's engine with a different MLP step. The
union states in each layer's weights which MLP it runs; the dense arm is the 27B's code as it was.

Rejected:
- A separate `qwen3_5_moe` family like `lfm2_moe`: a second copy of the DeltaNet layers, attention, rounds and
  host (about 3,000 lines), or a cross-family import of the 27B's loop.
- Running the 35B on the Qwen3.5 family's dense 2B Metal engine: it has no prompt cache, drafter or image path,
  so slices 2 and 3 would be rebuilt there. The config, expert loader and adapter still belong in that family.
- A trimmed copy of the 27B's round code: no change to the 27B, but every later fix made twice.
- The round code generic over the model (`Runner(comptime M)`): one copy, but a type parameter through about
  3,000 lines for a difference in the MLP step and a few pinned numbers.
- An optional MLP hook in the mixer table: close, but a hook hides which MLP a layer runs.

## The family's slices

1. Text, with lanes and the prompt cache (this PR).
2. Images on the checkpoint's own tower, which has the 27B's shape (27 blocks, 1,152 wide, 16 heads, patch 16,
   merge 2, no deepstack) apart from its last projection (2,048 wide against 5,120), on the 27B's image path.
3. MTP drafts from the checkpoint's own head, with #856's contract.
4. 8-bit experts.
5. (Optional) the z-lab DFlash drafter, with its own direct and full-token checks.

items.title: glm/cuda: KV pages from the core pool, kept states sized by their position (#1142)
items.body:
## What this changes

Implements #1142. GLM-5.3-Flash on CUDA gave every stream a window of KV, 13,056 bytes a token on every rank, so a 1M window held 12.75 GiB a rank for any conversation, and every kept prompt state copied a whole window. As proposed in #1142, the streams past the engine's own now take 512-row pages from the core `kv_pool` (#781), as Nemotron's do since #935. A kept state takes only the rows up to its position (piece 1 of #1142), which #993 brought to every stream in 1.1.2; a paged stream's rows go into #993's snapshot pages page by page.

`TF_KV_PAGES=auto`, the default, pages from three ranks up and keeps a window per stream at one and two ranks. That differs from Nemotron's default; question 1 below says why and asks about it.

Rebased on main after 1.1.2 (`f8d254c5`). The receipts below ran commit 11, and the raw ones are in `docs/receipts/glm-kv-pages-0b094b74/`.

Commits:

1. `2671de38` core: `kv_pool.split` with `snap_bytes == 0` means a family without snapshot slots, whose whole prompt cache is copied rows; `cuda_kv_pool.kept()` then uses the paged plan's `copied`. Without it the cache came from what window-sized streams leave, which on pages is nothing.
2. `2ee34d6b` `tf_glm_lat_write`, `tf_glm_pool_keys`, `tf_glm_scores` and `tf_glm_chunks_16/32` take a page table and the page stride, as Nemotron's attention takes `pt`. A null table reads the contiguous rows, as the engine's own sequence does. The chunk kernels load a window's keys in main's loop and a paged stream's keys in a loop of their own, chosen once a call: a helper that returned a pointer and branched on the table inside the `cp.async` loop made nvcc unroll that loop less even without a table. The other kernels look a page up once a block or a stage. The FP8 cache's kernels take no table, and their launchers refuse one.
3. `ff307818` A paged sequence (its fixed part, a page table, no cache rows of its own) and `Pages`: the page arena, the paged sequences, leases, table uploads, the NaN fill and the idle census. #993's snapshot plan takes a paged sequence's rows page by page (below). Host tests on a fake driver.
4. `804c4da3` The family's `kv_pool.Layout`, `attach`, admission, `TF_KV_PAGES` and `TF_KV_POISON`, and the ranks (a `pool` step, page ids on the `begin` step). With `--kv-cache fp8` the streams keep their windows (below).
5. `8e279c85` `tf-cuda-test glm-paged-check`: a paged stream against a whole-window twin, byte for byte.
6. `ae8a5a62` The other ranks make rank 0's pool through `Pages.follow`, which refuses a page size other than rank 0's (`RankMismatch`) before it allocates anything; a host test drives it on the fake driver.
7. `b7fecb3d` On pages too the chunk kernels read keys in main's loop: a dense chunk's 512 keys are one page, so a block points its key rows at that page once, and `tf_glm_dsa_tokens` writes a paged stream's selected tokens as their rows in the pool's pages (a table read a token, once a selection), which the sparse pass reads as main reads the tokens. With commit 2's own loop for pages, long prompts on pages ran 2.0 to 2.5% slower than main, all of it in the MLA stage by `TF_GLM_PROF`.
8. `786fabe8` The six kernels under the kernel contract, on a page table that is out of order and skips pages, with the cache's part past its page's start as a second cache's is in the pool: `tf_glm_lat_write` and `tf_glm_pool_keys` write onto pages, `tf_glm_scores` reads the pooled keys from them, `tf_glm_dsa_tokens` writes the selected tokens' rows, and `tf_glm_chunks_16` and `tf_glm_chunks_32`, dense and sparse, run through `tf_glm_merge` against a float64 softmax: eight registrations. `docs/kernel-contract.md` lists them, and `tf_glm_scores`' NaN under Known findings (below). Tests and docs only.
9. `c38f6d0b` Gate 5's records for the six launches: nvcc 13.0's usage, read from every SM's image (sm_80, 86, 89, 120 and 121), in `glm_cuda_records.cuda`, and nvcc 13.3's where it differs (four launches) in a `cuda_133` set the registry adds to 13.3's; the contract's image list takes `glm_ops` for `tf_glm_dsa_tokens`. Records and docs only.
10. `3b41fd7c` Tests for two guards of the paged snapshot code that had none, found by breaking each (below): a paged part's piece that starts inside a page's span keeps its offset there, and while a paged stream is current a prefix's size is the engine's own sequence's. Tests only.
11. `0b094b74` A stream takes its pages before its sequence is bound. With `TF_KV_PAGES=all` the engine's own sequence stays idle, so `--parallel N` has N - 1 paged sequences. Requests that arrive together are admitted before any of them opens, and the last to open took slot N: binding it made a whole-window sequence on rank 0 (12.88 GiB at a 1M window) before the pages refused it with `LaneMemory`. Now that slot waits for a paged sequence and nothing is made for it. Found by the first TP=3 run (below); at TP=2 the same path made a 1.77 GiB window inside the reserve, so the earlier TP=2 replies were equal. With a host test.
12. `cbe29802` That commit's comment on one line, as the lean check asks.
13. `2ce601ce` The raw receipts in `docs/receipts/glm-kv-pages-0b094b74/`: the logs and JSON of the runs below, with machine names, internal addresses and local paths replaced, and TP=3's `tp3/ring.patch` (below). Docs only.
14. `d7ff6494` Two stack traces in that receipt's mutation logs indented with spaces, as the desktop job's `git diff --check` asks. Docs only.

### On main after 1.1.2

- #993 sizes a kept state by its committed prefix, which this pull request's first commit did before the rebase, so that commit is gone and kept states are #993's. A paged sequence's latent rows and pooled keys go into #993's snapshot pages page by page through its table, in the same bytes and order as a window's prefix, and its page table stays its own, so a state kept on one kind of sequence resumes on the other. Index ring rows are copied as #993 copies them. A paged sequence holds its own request's rows only, so `snap_bytes` sizes a prefix on the engine's own sequence while a paged one is bound. A host test in `test-glm-snapshots-host` keeps a window's prefix, resumes it on a paged sequence whose pages are out of order, and back, and checks every field and row against the two layouts; two more check a piece that starts inside a page's span, which that test's small state never makes, and the size asked while a paged sequence is current.
- `--kv-cache fp8` keeps a window per stream: with it `auto` does not page, and `on` and `all` are refused by name (`Fp8OnPages`). Question 3 below asks how you would like FP8 rows on pages.
- #1053 is in main: `pool` follows its `idle` and #993's `snapshots` in `cuda_follow.zig`'s `Kind`. #1050 is open and touches `cuda_dsa_block.zig`, `cuda_engine.zig`, `cuda_native.zig` and `cuda_state.zig` in other hunks; whichever lands second is rebased on the first. Both also load the `glm_glue` module in `contract_tests.zig`'s `run`, in hunks git can merge without a conflict, so the second to land uses the first's module rather than a second `var glm_glue`; and both add `glm_glue` launch records to `glm_cuda_records.zig`.

### Against #1142

- Page size 512 rows (question 2), page ids sent by rank 0 (question 3) and the engine's own sequence kept at a full window and counted once (question 4), the defaults #1142 proposed.
- The pooled keys' `capacity/4 + 2` rows: the two extra rows are `pool_keys`' launch slack (grid `rows/4 + 2`). The kernel writes complete pools only (`4p + 3 <= pos + rows - 1`) and `scores` reads visible pools only (`p < (pos + r + 1)/4`), both inside `capacity/4`, so pages carry no slack. `selectTokens`' `np_max_cap` stays `capacity/4` on pages.

### Layout

- A page holds, for each of the 12 caches (11 DSA layers and the MTP layer), 512 latent rows (512 × 1,024 B) and their 128 pooled keys (128 × 256 B): 6,684,672 bytes, 512 × 13,056.
- Row `r` of a cache is at `pt[r / 512] * page + (r % 512) * 1,024` from the cache's base in the page, pooled key `p` at `pt[p / 128] * page + (p % 128) * 256`. A dense chunk is 512 keys, one page, so a block looks its page up once. A `scores` warp stages 16 pools from a multiple of 16 and a page holds 128, so it stays in one page. A sparse key's row comes from the token list, where `tf_glm_dsa_tokens` writes it as a row in the pages (commit 7).
- A stream's fixed part: KDA's conv and two recurrent copies, the window's scratch, the index rings (4,096 rows × 12 caches), its position, its first-draft row and its page table: 180 MiB at TP=2, as #1142's table.
- The engine's own sequence (slot 0) keeps its whole window, as Nemotron's: the lone stream's path and its bits are unchanged.

### Admission and ranks

- `attach`: rank 0 plans the pool by the smallest rank's room and sends a `pool` step (streams, pages, page bytes). Every rank makes the same paged sequences and page arena; a page size that differs between ranks is refused by name (`RankMismatch`).
- A request takes `ceil((prompt + max_tokens + 16) / 512)` pages when it starts and gives them back when it ends. Its page ids ride its `begin` step; the other ranks write them to their tables and never take pages of their own.
- `fits`: the engine's own sequence is free, or a paged sequence is free and the pool holds the request's pages. Otherwise the lane host puts the request back (`LaneMemory`) until a stream ends.
- A stream takes its pages before its sequence is bound (commit 11): requests admitted together can outnumber the free paged sequences, and the one past them waits (`LaneMemory`) with no sequence made for its slot.
- When every stream has ended, rank 0 logs `kv pool idle: promised 0, free N + store 0 == total N`.

### `TF_KV_PAGES`

- `auto` (or unset): `on` from three ranks up, `off` at one and two.
- `on` (any value but the others, as Nemotron reads `TF_KV_PAGES`): every stream past the engine's own on pages.
- `off` or `0`: a window per stream, as before (`0` is Nemotron's word for it).
- `all`: every stream on pages, the engine's own sequence left idle, for checks (one stream fewer at once than `--parallel`).
- `TF_KV_POISON=1`: a stream's pages are NaN until its rows are written.

Rank 0 alone reads `TF_KV_PAGES`; the other ranks follow its `pool` step. Each rank reads `TF_KV_POISON` for its own pages. With `--kv-cache fp8`, `auto` and `off` give windows, and `on` and `all` are refused (`Fp8OnPages`).

## Questions

1. **The prompt cache before pages, at two ranks.** `kv_pool.plan` funds a page a stream, then the prompt cache, then the other pages. On two GB10s the room left after the weights and the engine's own window is 6 to 9 GiB, under the default 16 GiB cache, so with `on` the pool would be three pages. A request reserves the pages of its prompt and its `max_tokens`, so most concurrent requests would wait for the engine's own sequence: fewer streams at once than with windows. That is why `auto` keeps windows at TP=2, and why the TP=2 receipts below set `--prompt-cache-gib 4`. Would you rather the plan fund pages before the cache up to a floor (the pages of one request at `--context`, or a share of the room)? Then `on` could be the default at every rank count, as for Nemotron.
2. **The engine's own window on pages (#1142's question 4).** GLM on CUDA captures no graphs, so the reason Nemotron keeps its own sequence at a full window does not apply here. That window is 12.75 GiB a rank at a 1M window (1,048,640 rows × 13,056 B) and about 3 GiB at TP=2's 245,760. If the plan keeps room for one window of pages, so that one conversation can still reach `--context`, the peak stays the same; what changes is that those bytes serve the other streams while the engine's own conversation is short. It needs `kv_pool.plan` to count the engine's own sequence on pages (a `Budget` field; Nemotron's behavior unchanged) and slot 0 to become a paged sequence. If you agree, we add it to this pull request; if not, it stays as #935 has it. #1211 builds this, stacked on this pull request, so you can see it before you decide.
3. **FP8 rows on pages.** With 1.1.2's `--kv-cache fp8` a cache keeps 512 E4M3 bytes a row and, after all its rows, one FP32 scale a row. On pages the rows would go 512 to a page as BF16 rows do, and a row's scale is easiest found beside its own page's rows: each 512-row block would keep its scales after its rows. Would you have windows keep the same blocks, so that a window is pages in order and one address formula serves both? Until you say, this pull request keeps FP8 caches on windows; FP8 on pages would follow with its kernels' registration.

## Receipt

On this head (`d7ff6494`, on main `f8d254c5`). Every run on one GPU and at TP=2 used the binaries built from commit 11 (`0b094b74`); commits 12 to 14 put a comment on one line and add the raw receipts. The kernel contract ran on `3b41fd7c` (commit 10): commit 11 changes no kernel. TP=3's ranks ran commit 11's engine source (the first TP=3 run, which found the bug, `b7fecb3d`'s) with two commits our ring of three GB10s needs, which are not part of this pull request (`tp3/ring.patch` in the receipts): rank 0's NCCL id handed to the other ranks in a file, so that a ring of /32 links bootstraps (#1178 does it upstream's way), and a heat ceiling (`TF_HEAT_CEILING`: a prompt chunk also waits while its expected rise would pass the ceiling), which changes when chunks run, not what they compute.

items.title: glm/cuda: the engine's own sequence on KV pages too, one window of them planned first (stacked on #1163)
items.body:
## What this changes

Builds #1163's question 2. With `TF_KV_PAGES` paging (`auto` from three ranks up, `on`), the engine's own sequence (slot 0) takes pages from the core pool too, so no stream holds a whole window. The plan sets one window of pages aside first, so one conversation can still reach `--context`; while the engine's own conversation is short, those pages serve the other streams. At TP=3 with a 1M window, the pool goes from 1,284 pages beside the engine's 12.88 GiB window to 3,355 pages for all eight streams (receipt below).

Stacked on #1163: its 14 commits come first, unchanged, and this pull request's own are the last seven (15 to 21). Until #1163 lands, the diff shows both. If you would rather have these in #1163, I will move them to its branch.

Commits:

15. `62e2aeb3` core `kv_pool`: `Budget.engine_paged`, false for Nemotron, whose tests pass unchanged. When it is true, `plan` takes one window of pages (`pages(window)`, the floor) from the room first, then the other streams' fixed parts and a page each, the prompt cache, and the rest as pages, at most `(1 + others) × pages(window)`. A room under the floor is `NoStream`. `holds` counts the same way.
16. `7d4f8dc8` native: `Loaded.engine_paged` goes to `plan` and `holds`, and the startup line and the `NoStream` message say so (below).
17. `8737d30d` GLM declares `window_rows` (8) to the native server. Without it the plan's window was the context alone, so `pages(window)` could be one page short of a request's longest page table (16 against 17 at a context of 8,192), and the floor depends on it.
18. `b216a74b` A kept prefix's size (`Plan.size`) counts its rows to the capacity, whatever pages are mapped. `cuda_snapshots.bytes` measured a prefix on the engine's own window while a paged stream was current; with no window anywhere it would return the maximum, and the prompt cache would keep nothing, silently.
19. `27feda8b` The engine's own sequence on pages: `Engine.init` makes slot 0 a paged sequence with no rows of its own; `Pages` covers slots 0 to N − 1 and places slot 0 on the arena (`State.place`), refusing a slot 0 that holds a window (`OwnNotPaged`); every rank resolves `TF_KV_PAGES`, and the ranks agree on it (`Settings.pages`, `Fingerprint.pages`, layout 12); `all` becomes `on`, and the lanes lose `all`'s idle slot.
20. `8e705835` `glm-paged-check`'s paged stream is slot 0, on pages from its init; its whole-window twin stays in slot 3.
21. `87e4417e` The raw receipts in `docs/receipts/glm-kv-pages-8e705835/`. Docs only.

### What changes for a launch

- Every rank reads `TF_KV_PAGES`, and the ranks agree on it at startup: ranks that resolve it differently stop with `TF_KV_PAGES` named. In #1163 rank 0 alone read it, so a launch that set it on rank 0 only now sets it on every rank.
- `all` is `on`: with the engine's own sequence on pages there is no idle slot, and `--parallel N` serves N streams on pages.
- The startup line: "8 streams at once, the engine's own and 7 more taking 3355 pages of 512 rows (20.89 GiB) as they need them (enough for one at a 1048576-token window), 131 MiB fixed each, of 37.8 GiB left after a 12.2 GiB reserve". When the room does not hold the floor: "the CUDA memory budget fits no stream beside the model: one at a W-token window takes X GiB of KV pages, and the budget leaves Y GiB".
- Windows are unchanged: `off`, `auto` at one and two ranks, and `--kv-cache fp8`.

### #1163's question 1

With the engine's own sequence on pages, the plan funds one window of pages before the prompt cache, the floor question 1 asked about, so `on` always keeps room for one conversation to reach `--context`. The rest of question 1, whether `auto` should page at one and two ranks, stays open: this pull request keeps windows there.

## Receipt

On this head (`87e4417e`, on #1163's head `d7ff6494`, on main `f8d254c5`). Every run on one GPU and at TP=2 used the binaries built from commit 20 (`8e705835`); commit 21 adds the raw receipts. TP=3's ranks ran commit 20's engine source with the two commits our ring of three GB10s needs that #1163's receipt describes (`tp3/ring.patch`). The kernels are #1163's, unchanged, so its kernel contract and gate 5's records stand; the environment is #1163's (GB10s, sm_121, driver 580.178.04, NCCL 2.30.7, Zig 0.17.0, nvcc 13.3.73, `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4@423acf37`).

- Exactness:
  - `tf-cuda-test glm-paged-check` on the checkpoint's first five layers, its paged stream now the engine's own sequence on pages from its init: at TP=2, at TP=3 and on one GPU, 7 prompts at the pages' edges and 91 window rows equal their whole-window twins' logits, tokens and drafts byte for byte, the pages out of order (12 jumps) and NaN before use, the pool idle after; the other ranks made rank 0's pool and mapped its pages through every step. The synthetic checkpoint's checks pass (`glm-ref`, `glm-synth`, `glm-lanes-cover`, `glm-lanes-concurrent`, `glm-shared-check`, `glm-paged-check`).
  - Served at TP=2, `--context 131072 --parallel 4 --prompt-cache-gib 4 TF_KV_POISON=1`: `TF_KV_PAGES=all` and `on`, now one configuration ("4 streams at once, the engine's own and 3 more taking 803 pages of 512 rows (5.00 GiB) as they need them (enough for one at a 131072-token window), 180 MiB fixed each"; #1163 had 504 pages with the engine's own sequence idle, or 509 beside its window): 12 cells each, every reply equal to its alone run (28/28) and to `"draft": false` (30/30), each record's 44 requests cached as planned. The `on` record replayed on this head's windows (`auto` keeps them at TP=2) and on main `f8d254c5`: against the `on` and the `all` records, 43/43 replies equal and as cached as planned in all four, drafted == plain 23/23, no resumed reply slower than its fresh one. Images on pages (561 pages): the same tokens drafted, repeated, with `"draft": false` and three at once, and a chat resumed past its image (6,144 of 7,603 tokens cached) equals its cold run.
  - Served at TP=3, `--parallel 8`, `TF_KV_POISON=1` on pages:
    - `TF_KV_PAGES` unset at a 1M window: "8 streams at once, the engine's own and 7 more taking 3355 pages of 512 rows (20.89 GiB) as they need them (enough for one at a 1048576-token window), 131 MiB fixed each, of 37.8 GiB left after a 12.2 GiB reserve" (#1163's: 1,284 pages beside the engine's 12.88 GiB window). 16 cells, every reply equal to its alone run (60/60) and to `"draft": false` (72/72); the record's 44 requests cached as planned; cold prompts of 1k to 64k in 0.73 s to 43.4 s, as #1163's; seven 2k prompts sent while a 64k conversation held its rows on pages (63,488 of its 65,536 tokens resumed): all seven equal their alone runs, and none waited.
    - `TF_KV_PAGES=all` at a 96k window: 1,544 pages, the bound of eight windows' pages. 60/60 and 72/72, and in the cells of eight no request waited (the longest first token 1.69 to 2.15 s; under #1163's `all` the eighth waited, 12.0 to 21.2 s).
    - `TF_KV_PAGES=off --prompt-cache-gib 0 --parallel auto` at a 1M window: two windows, as before. The `auto` record replayed there: 43/43, drafted == plain 23/23.
    - The pool at its floor: `TF_KV_PAGES=all` at a 96k window, asking a 37.2 GiB prompt cache. The plan trims the cache to 35.9 GiB to keep the floor and a page a stream, 200 pages. Three 64k prompts (129 pages each) alone, then together: all three equal their alone runs, each resumed 63,488 of its 65,536 tokens, and they ran one at a time.
  - After every stream ends, each idle census reads `free N + store 0 == total N`: 3,355, 1,544 and 200 at TP=3; 803, 757 and 561 at TP=2.
- Speed at TP=2 against main `f8d254c5` on the same two GB10s, the serves alternating: this head, main, this head, main, then this head with every stream on pages (`TF_KV_PAGES=all`), each at `--context 131072 --parallel 4 --prompt-cache-gib 0`. Seconds, lower is better; a ratio is this head's faster serve over main's slower.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: NVFP4 experts on prompt tiles with the decode form's sums, bit for bit
items.body:
## What this changes

On a ModelOpt NVFP4 checkpoint (`nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local`, local-inference-lab's and Mia-AiLab's exports)
the routed experts of a prompt chunk ran the decode kernel: `nvfp4_expert_kernel` on plans of 16 pairs an item, so a
1,536-row chunk (about 30 pairs an expert) read each expert's weights two to three times, through a kernel without
shared-memory staging. The prompt tiles `nvfp4_experts.cu` already has (`tf_nvfp4_prompt_*`, Nemotron's) sum
differently (codes times scales in bf16, one fp32 sum over K) and have no fp32 down, so they could not stand in.

- `prompt_tiles` gets a `FACT` flag. With it each 16-input block is one mma of the raw codes from zero and then
  `fma(p, its e4m3 scale, acc)`, blocks in ascending K, then the global scale and the epilogue: the decode form's
  arithmetic in its order, so every row's bits are the decode form's at any row count. Without it the code is as
  before; the 55 existing functions' SASS is identical to `main`'s on sm_80, 86, 89, 120 and 121.
- Two entries: `tf_nvfp4_fact_swiglu` (SwiGLU gate-up to bf16, 4 warps) and `tf_nvfp4_fact_down_f32` (fp32 slot rows,
  8 warps), on plans of `promptTile(.nvfp4)` = 64 pairs an item; `Nvfp4Experts.runFact` launches them.
- `cuda_batch.zig`'s ModelOpt expert path takes them from 64 rows a pass (`TF_FLASHNEXT_FACT_ROWS`, 0 for never);
  below it, decode rounds and verify windows, nothing changes. Since the bits are the same either way, the threshold
  only sets speed.

Overlap: Mirrdhyn's #1046 does this for the MLX affine experts (`flashnext_fexp.cu`, factored g32 tiles) and the
format-independent prompt kernels; it does not touch the ModelOpt NVFP4 experts. This branch is off `main` and stacks
on nothing of #1046; the two touch different expert formats, and `cuda_batch.zig`'s `moeBlockKeep` in different
branches of its `if (lw.native_experts)`.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `main` `d1018b31` plus this branch; one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0, nvcc 13.0.88);
  checkpoint `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local@b9ce18a6` (33/33 files against the publisher's hashes).
- Exactness:
  - `tf-cuda-test nvfp4-fact`: random NVFP4 experts (dims 256, width 160, 6 experts), gate-up and fp32 down from the
    fact tiles on 64-pair plans byte-equal to the decode form on 16-pair plans at 1, 7, 17, 22, 64, 65, 130 and 300
    rows; each output within its float64 bound (worst 0.47 of it for gate-up, 0.01 for down). Control: the existing
    scaled-code prompt tile on the same plan parts from the decode form's bytes (red).
  - Served, greedy, against `main` on the same checkpoint and flags: every reply byte-identical (three chats, three
    ~8k agent contexts, one 30,922-token context; 64-96 tokens each).
- Prompt speed (cold, `--no-drafts --parallel 4 --context 40960`, `--prompt-cache-gib 0`, time to first token):

  | prompt | main | this | |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | 7,459 tokens | 6.09 s | 5.30 s | 0.87x |
  | 7,938 tokens | 6.51 s | 5.76 s | 0.88x |
  | 8,222 tokens | 6.96 s | 6.13 s | 0.88x |
  | 30,922 tokens | 25.74 s | 22.60 s | 0.88x |

  Per-op GPU time of a 1,536-row chunk (cudaEvents around each op class, a local measurement patch): routed experts
  480 ms on `main`, 330 ms here (every expert's 2.76 MB of weights read once an item; 68 GB a chunk, a 250 ms floor at
  the GB10's bandwidth). With `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK=4096` the weights are read once per 4,096 rows: 8k prompts 4.73-5.39 s,
  30,922 tokens 19.93 s, replies again identical (the chunk size is not changed here).
- Decode speed: unchanged (23.6 / 23.6 tok/s code / chat at one stream, 65.6 / 64.9 aggregate at four, `main` 23.6 /
  23.7 and 65.6 / 65.1); decode rows never reach 64.
- Kernel contract, `tf-cuda-test kernel-contract` (built `-Dnvcc`, ReleaseFast) on the GB10: `SUMMARY 87 kernels: 87 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail, 0 known findings; 8 controls: 8 red as planted, 0 missed; 1533 limit problems` (this run less the 2 entries and the control is 85 kernels and 7 controls; the 1,533 limit problems also appear on a main-based run on this box (another branch, same count), none in the two new launches, which pass live on sm_121)
  - 2 new entries (`zig/tests/cuda/contract_nvfp4_fact.zig`), each a replacement of the decode instance it stands for
    (`nvfp4_expert_kernel<2, 2, 4>`, `<1, 0, 4>`): gate 3 bit-equal at Flash Next's shapes (2,560 dims, 640 wide)
    and the tile edges; gate 1 by the stated rule (the decode form's bytes with NaN and infinite global scales, a NaN
    block scale, NaN and infinite inputs, some output non-finite); gate 4 on integer inputs whose partial sums reach
    about 2^20; SwiGLU states `sums.bf16 = 30`: a bf16 sum that collapses moves the output by about itself, and the epilogue's three bf16 roundings already allow 3u of it, so at most 85x is provable (measured: fp16 misses 1,192,211x, bf16 36x; the fp32 down: 272,629,752x and 1,962,934,214x).
  - Control: the scaled-code prompt tile registered as the decode gate-up's replacement, red at gate 3.
  - Gate 5: 2 launches recorded from nvcc 13.0.88 cubins for sm_80, 86, 89, 120a and 121a; live on sm_121 both match.
    The run's 1,533 limit problems are `main`'s (the offline audit of every recorded launch on this nvcc).
  - `tf_nvfp4_fact_swiglu` takes 255 registers and spills 116 bytes on sm_121 (the existing SwiGLU prompt tile none).
- Tests run: `zig build test --summary all` (built `-Dnvcc`): 211/211 steps succeeded (the summary counts 1,462 of 1,465 tests passed, 3 skipped); `tf-cuda-test nvfp4-fact` and `kernel-contract`; `zig fmt --check` clean.
- Not run, and why: sm_80/86/89/120 only through their compiles (gate 5); Metal (no Metal change).

## Gotchas

- **Overlap with #1046:** it doesn't touch the ModelOpt NVFP4 experts, but both edit `cuda_batch.zig`'s `moeBlockKeep`, in different branches of the same `if`. #1046 itself conflicts with `main` right now, so I measured it on its own 1.1.0 base and didn't stack on it.
- **Conflict with #1147** (no zero fills): one hunk in the same expert path. Keep this PR's routing and `runFact`, and wrap the `cuMemsetD8Async` in #1147's `if (native.world != 1 or native.rank != 0)`.
- **Register pressure:** `tf_nvfp4_fact_swiglu` takes 255 registers and spills 116 bytes on sm_121. It is still faster, and tuning comes next.
- **Prompt gap:** this closes only part of it. vLLM on the related mtpfp4 checkpoint takes 2.9-3.7 s for an 8k prompt, against 5.3-6.1 s here. FP4 activations don't close it (see question 3); the rest is the hyper-connections, DeltaNet and the router.
- **Untested:** sm_80/86/89/120 are compile-only.

## Questions

These came up while measuring and are your call, not part of this change:

1. `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK=4096` instead of the default 1,536 rows takes another 11-12 % off prompts on this checkpoint (numbers above), with identical replies. The cost is about 2.3 GiB more and a longer pause for other streams' decode per chunk (about 3 s instead of 1.1 s). Should the default move, or stay an option?
2. `TF_FLASHNEXT_DRAFT_HEAD=affine4` is 10-13 % faster drafted at one stream on this checkpoint (code and chat), outputs equal. Should it become the default for ModelOpt checkpoints?
3. ~~Would an opt-in `--precision checkpoint` for Flash Next be welcome?~~ Withdrawn: I built it locally (FP4xFP4 experts under the checkpoint's input scales), and it gave no speed. At these chunk sizes the experts are bound by streaming their weights, so FP4 math saves nothing, and the extra quantize passes cost a little. It also couldn't be quality-gated, because the Flash Next backend returns no logprobs.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false` (8/8), concurrent equals solo (8/8), and a resumed two-turn prompt equals a fresh one (7,147 of 7,184 tokens restored), each equal to `main`'s output (MTP drafts on, `--prompt-cache-gib 4`; measured at `074e0ec3`, before the later lean fix, which only folds comments and moves code).
- [x] No precision traded for speed. The bits do not change.
- [x] A new or changed GPU kernel is registered with the kernel contract; the `SUMMARY` line is in the receipt.
- [x] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release (0.87-0.88x of `main`).
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran: CUDA on GB10 (sm_121) live; sm_80/86/89/120 through their compiles only; no Metal change.
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency (`nvfp4-fact`'s control is red on the old tile).
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

"On v1.1.2" below has what the rebase changed and what was retaken on it; the rest of this description and `docs/receipts/` are the v1.1.1 line's and name its commits, except where they name v1.1.2.

`nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local` loads as stored and serves on CUDA at TP=2 and TP=3, on v1.1.1. The tested implementation, called this head below, is `80517fc3` (eight commits), with its receipt in `c595d643`. Seven code commits follow the receipt. Three change comments and docs, the loader gate's own checks, and `capabilities`' format names and the refusal texts (checked on `d23862ab`; `839a32f7` adds those checks to the receipt with video serves taken on this head, and two more receipt-only commits reword its video row and replace local names in its tools). Four change what the loader does or what is tested: the loader refuses by name, before its upload, an FP8 projection that a GPU without clusters could not run; `readRecipes` returns a failed read or allocation as an error, not as a config without recipes; a test holds `csfLinear`'s refusal of an empty weight; and the kernel contract has a control for the float32 norm weight. TP=3 and the rest of the receipt were not retaken on `797dd2e1`. On this head, the served exactness checks (golden, concurrent, resume, prompts sent together) pass on both checkpoints at TP=2 and TP=3; media, video (with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, #1107) and structured output pass on both at TP=2, and media on FP4-Local at TP=3; the loader gate and the lanes checks ran on FP4-Local at both. ## What this changes

The CUDA GLM-5.3-Flash family loads `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local` (#1015, #593 (4)) as stored, with bf16 activations into every layer, and serves it, checked here at TP=2 and TP=3 on v1.1.1 and in part at TP=2 on v1.1.2 ("On v1.1.2" above). It is on v1.1.2 (`4ff78441`), rebased from v1.1.1 (`b10231b9`), which has #1021 to #1024's host foundations, and uses #907 and #908 from 1.1.0.

Beyond the summary's first table:

- Formats: before it computes a width, an element count or a block count, the classifier refuses an empty shape (`EmptyShape`) and one whose arithmetic would overflow (`ShapeOverflow`). A checkpoint without recipes (`nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`) reads as before; a read of config.json that fails after the entry has admitted it, or an allocation that fails while the loader reads the recipes, is an error, never a config without recipes, whose modules would then read as declared NVFP4. A test now holds `csfLinear`'s own refusal of an empty weight (`EmptyShape`); in the loader the classifier refuses such a weight first.
- FP8 lanes: on a GPU without thread block clusters (before sm_90) the lane would sum an FP8 projection's K slices as partials in memory, and the GLM forward holds none, so the loader now refuses such a projection by name before packing or uploading it; before, matmul refused it only at the first forward, after the whole load. On sm_90 and later, GB10 included, the lane never needs those partials, so the check refuses nothing.
- The routed experts' `csf_32x2_v1` scales need no kernel change. The MTP layer's bf16 routed experts are still quantized on the GPU.
- KDA's MXFP8 `[q | k | v]` and bf16 `[f_a | g_a | b]` each run into their columns of the stack's rows. A bf16 widening of an MXFP8 tensor (the MTP layer's `kv_b`, and `lm_head` for the draft head's quantizer) loads only when every value is exact in bf16, else it is refused by name.
- On prompt rows a bf16 head runs as before; the MXFP8 `lm_head`'s K split depends on the shape alone, so a row's bits do not depend on how many rows run with it.
- The `_f32w` forms run the bf16 forms' arithmetic on a float32 weight, so a float32 norm adds no launch. On 1.1.0's tree the bf16 forms compiled to the same SASS as before (all 40 `glm_glue` functions on sm_121, nvcc 13.0), and `hc_finish_f32w` is checked against a float64 reference through Sinkhorn.
- Docs: `docs/quantization.md`'s "GLM-5.3-Flash's float32 tensors on CUDA" names the float32 tensors the loader keeps in float32 and says that any other, which 1.1.1 rounded to bf16, loads as bf16 only when bf16 holds every value and is otherwise refused by name. The rule refuses none of the NVFP4 and FP4-Local checkpoints' float32 tensors, and the EXL3/TR3 checkpoint's float32 tensors are all of the kinds kept in float32.
- Vision: the tower's quantized projections give fp32 or bf16 outputs; bf16 projections and the attention products stay on cuBLASLt, and a tower without recipes (the NVFP4 checkpoint's) reads as before. `tools/glm_vision_ref.py` reads such projections back to the float32 values their codes and scales hold.
- `glm-loader-gate` compares at TP 1, 2 and 3 against a separately opened checkpoint (csf decoded by the gate itself; NVFP4, MXFP8 and block-FP8 tiles from the host packers). `TF_GATE_LAYERS`, `TF_GATE_WORLDS` and `TF_GATE_RANKS` narrow a real checkpoint's run, and a run that gates no rank or compares no upload fails. `TF_GATE_TAMPER` flips one upload's bit, and the run passes only red as planted: every gated rank reports that upload, and nothing else.
- Capabilities: the family lists `modelopt-mixed` (FlashNext's name for ModelOpt's MIXED_PRECISION) beside `modelopt-nvfp4`, and the refusal of another quantization names NVFP4 and MIXED_PRECISION.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: the PLE gather keeps a parked worker pool instead of spawning threads per call
items.body:
## What this changes

Flash Next's PLE n-gram gather (`Ngram.rows` in `families/flashnext/cuda_ple.zig`) spawned `min(128, items / 4)` threads per call and joined them. The gather itself is a few memcpys from the mapped table, so most of a call was thread start-up: about 65-80 µs per thread, 150 µs for one decode token, 1 ms for a 4-token batch (4 streams, or a drafted verify) and 10-11 ms per prompt chunk.

The table now keeps a pool for its life (`cuda_ple_pool.zig`, 139 lines with a unit test):
- workers are spawned on first need, up to 127, and park on a futex between calls; `deinit` wakes and joins them;
- a call's parts are the same `[lo, hi)` ranges as before, claimed from one counter by the caller and the workers. Each claim that leaves parts unclaimed wakes one more worker, so quick parts stay mostly on the caller and slow (faulting) parts fan out;
- calls are serialised by a mutex, and the first failed part's error is returned, in part order, as before.

Only which thread copies a range changes, so the output bytes are identical by construction. A table without a pool (for example a path that builds `Ngram` some other way) gathers on the caller's thread.

Branch `fn-ple-pool` @ `e4062e6a`, on `main` @ `bd264368a`.

## Receipt

- **Environment.** One GB10 (sm_121), CUDA 13.0, Zig 0.17.0. `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` @ `b9ce18a6` (its `tensors/` index loads since #1179).
- **`rows()` on the real table**, p50, alternating old / new / old / new, output hashes identical at every size:

| items | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 16 (one decode token) | 165 / 163 µs | 18 / 22 µs |
| 64 (4 tokens) | 1,020 / 971 µs | 31 / 32 µs |
| 4,096 | 11.4 / 10.4 ms | 0.95 / 0.97 ms |
| 8,192 | 11.5 / 10.7 ms | 1.66 / 1.66 ms |

- **Served**, a fresh server per arm, main / this PR / main / this PR with `--no-drafts`, then one MTP pair:

| | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| c=1 ms/step | 42.00 / 42.14 | 41.90 / 41.74 | -0.1 / -0.4 (noise-sized) |
| c=4 ms/step | 61.11 / 61.87 | 60.09 / 60.84 | -1.02 / -1.03 |
| TTFT 8k | 6.365 / 6.481 s | 6.335 / 6.432 s | -0.03 / -0.05 s |
| MTP c=1 ms/round (one run) | 60.52 | 59.44 | -1.08 |
| MTP c=4 ms/round (one run) | 223.6 | 218.9 | -4.7 (-2.1 %) |

  The c=4 gain has the same size and sign in both rounds. The microbench accounts for about 0.65 ms of it (4 lanes x 4 calls a round); the remaining ~0.35 ms is not explained. Prompt chunks mostly hide the old cost, because the batch path gathers on a side thread while the layers before the PLE layer run.
- **Exactness.** Token hashes for greedy c=1 and c=4, seeded c=1 and c=4, and both turns of a resumed prompt-cache run: identical across all six servers, the MTP ones included.
- **Tests.** Full `zig build test -Dnvcc=...` exit 0. lean_check 0 new. `zig fmt` clean.
- **Contract.** No kernel change.

- Metal: `cuda_ple.zig` belongs to the CUDA family only, so there was nothing to run there.
- The one-thread gather `cuda_batch.zig` starts per pass (~28 µs) could use the same pool; left for a separate change.

## Overlap

#1113 sets the thread count for its EXL3 table in the same function and builds that table without going through `Ngram.init`, so a rebase there needs a hand-merge; its table then simply gathers on the caller's thread, as before.

items.title: qwen CUDA: TF_DRAFT_NODES above 15 serves; a stop or cancel lands between prompt chunks
items.body:
Two serving fixes for the Qwen3.5 CUDA family, found on one RTX 5090 (Qwen3.8-27B MLX 4-bit + DFlash2, `--kv-cache fp8`, a 262,144-token window).

**`TF_DRAFT_NODES` above 15 failed every request.** The server started, then every round failed with `BadDraftFrame`. The planner asks a grown tree for its node budget as the hold's depth, and `cuda_draft_frame.stage` refused any depth past `block - 1`, a chain's limit. Grown trees (block 16, no planner lanes) now stage up to `tree.nodes()` (at most the 64-row window); chains and 8-row blocks keep `block - 1`. `TF_DRAFT_NODES=24` and `32` serve with every reply unchanged. A host test in `qwen35_draft_frame_host.zig` covers both limits and fails without the fix.

**A stop or a cancel waited for the whole prompt pass.** The CUDA prompt pass never asked `Stream.isCancelled`, so the host's halt (which joins the lane thread) waited until a long prefill finished: with a 230k-token prompt in progress the server stopped draining and did not exit, and a client that left mid-pass kept the GPU until the pass ended. The pass now asks before each chunk, as the other backends do; its cache goes back to the pool and is reset when taken again. With a 75,616-token prompt, SIGTERM 15 s into the pass exits after 23 s (the 20 s drain, then the next chunk) instead of 134 s, the request ending "server restarting: retry shortly"; a streaming client killed mid-pass ends its request within a second (`client-left`).

The Metal `qwen3_5` backend's prompt loop (`backend.zig`) has the same missing check; that is left to a Metal change.

Checks: `zig build test`, `test-kernel-contract`, `test-golden`, `fuzz-cortheon`, the Flash Next gate test, `zig fmt` and the lean check pass, as do the `test-qwen35-*` host steps.

items.title: glm cuda: rank 0's NCCL id goes over the ranks' lines, so a /32 ring's followers bootstrap on NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME
items.body:
## What this changes

GLM-5.3-Flash's CUDA ranks other than 0 take rank 0's NCCL unique id over the ranks' liveness lines (`cuda/tp_watch.zig`, which open before NCCL), as Flash Next's rank 1 takes its id over its link (`families/flashnext/cuda_collective.zig`) and the fabric's bootstrap broadcasts rank 0's (`fabric/tp/tp.zig`). A follower that names `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` also unsets `NCCL_COMM_ID` before its first NCCL call.

With `NCCL_COMM_ID` set, NCCL's bootstrap looks on every rank for a local interface in that address's subnet and does not read `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` (`bootstrapNetInit`). On hosts joined only by point-to-point links whose addresses are /32s routed over them, as our three GB10s in a switchless ring, only rank 0's host has one, so ranks 1 and 2 stop there (`NET/Socket : No usable listening interface found`) and TP=3 does not start. We raised this on #636 ([comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/636#issuecomment-6215248831)), planning to start GLM's ranks through the fabric's `Session.open`; this is a smaller step that keeps GLM's lines and `NCCL_COMM_ID` and moves only the id onto the lines. Until now we ran TP=3 with a local commit that passes the id through a file, as the GLM lanes tests' runner does (`zig/tests/cuda/glm_lanes_tests.zig`, `openComm`).

What stays: rank 0 makes the id from `NCCL_COMM_ID`, so the root listens where the operator put it, and `NCCL_COMM_ID` still names the lines' address on every host. A follower without `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` keeps `NCCL_COMM_ID`, and the id it now takes from its line is the one it used to make. For a follower that names `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME`, only the bootstrap moves to that interface: NCCL's net interfaces already took `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` first. An `NCCL_COMM_ID` line in `~/.nccl.conf` or `/etc/nccl.conf` comes back at NCCL's first call and keeps the old bootstrap.

The id goes in three records of the lines' 64-byte form, each a part number and up to 48 of the id's 128 bytes. A follower waits for all three up to 15 minutes, as for the ranks' ready records.
