items.title: qwen CUDA: Qwen3.8-27B decode 9-15% faster with DFlash2 (code +25%), replies unchanged
items.body:
Faster decode rounds for Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 on CUDA, and the lane planner's pricing of context copies. Measured on one RTX 5090 (MLX 4-bit + DFlash2, `--kv-cache fp8`, a 262,144-token window, one stream).

Ruler at one stream, tok/s (prose / code / structured / list):

| | prose | code | structured | list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 211.5 | 396.6 | 265.7 | 258.7 |
| this PR (before the copy pricing) | 243.3 | 450.8 | 293.6 | 283.5 |

Every reply on the ruler prompts is byte-identical to main's: the kernel changes keep each value's arithmetic and reduction order, and the drafter changes move only the drafts (verification decides every token).

**Kernels**
- `tf_q35d_dyn_conv_batch` on a (rows, channel blocks) grid instead of one block a row: 15.8 to 1.7 us.
- `tf_q35d_attn_partial`: four warps a 256-key chunk, keys split over the lanes, the ring row advanced instead of a 64-bit modulo a key, empty chunks returning at once: 92 to 15.5 us.
- `tf_q35_gdn_pre` writes a recorded window's conv log from the taps it already reads, so `tf_q35_conv_commit` only moves the stream's tail; its loads are 8-byte (3.8 to 2.9 us a layer).
- `tf_q35_gdn_slots_*` prefetch the next row and take two value rows a warp up to four slots (`slots_2` 17.4 to 14.3 us, `slots_4` 22.9 to 13.8 us).
- `tf_q35_norm` moves its row in 16-byte lanes through shared memory; each thread's sum of squares still reads its own entries in order (3.7 to 2.5 us).
- `tf_q35_gdn_post`, `tf_q35_attn_gate` and `tf_q35_mlp_act` write their outputs' 64-entry group sums (`group_sum`, in order), so the out, o and down projections no longer launch `tf_q35_sums` first: about 4,800 fewer launches a 256-token reply.

**Lane planner.** Live lone pricing (`lone_cost_tile`) kept each stream's measured round times and its losing widths' retry deadlines on the stream, so every request calibrated again with forced trials at one row (no drafts) and at the tile from round 8. The engine now keeps the newest calibration of a stream that only ran alone (greedy and sampled apart), and a stream's first priced round starts from it, its deadlines counted from that round. A stream that shared a round leaves nothing; one already priced keeps its own. This was 2-5% of the one-stream ruler. Only families with `lone_cost_tile` (Qwen CUDA) are affected; unit tests in `lone_costs_test.zig`. Kept calibrations are filed a context band each (under 8,192 tokens, then one a doubling, the last from 131,072 on), so a stream starts only from one measured at its own length, and a carried deadline or spacing reaches at most 256 rounds into the next stream. Without the bands, one greedy reply on a 252,783-token prompt left its 30 ms wide rounds as every later short stream's prices (the decode ruler's prose 238 tok/s and code 415 after it, against 253-257 and 495-496 with the bands, as on a fresh server, every reply byte-identical), and the doubled spacing of losing trials grew to thousands of rounds over a long run, so no stream re-timed the wide widths until a restart.

**Lane planner: context copies priced at the stream's own copy rate.** A lone head window that a context copy extends has more rows than the drafter grew, so the drafter could not price them and allocation fell back to chain probabilities from the stream's per-depth acceptance for every row, tree and copy alike. Those fall fast with depth, so a copy's tail looked hopeless and was cut: code replies, where copies from the prompt keep landing, verified 11.3 rows a round against about 14 elsewhere. The drafts now keep the drafter's own chances, and each copied row takes its parent's chance times the stream's copy rate: the rows its copies landed over those rows plus the chains that broke before their end (decayed 0.9 a round, primed from `cfg.copy_rate`'s 0.94 as sixteen rows' worth); a copy counts only when its anchor row landed. A unit test in `windows.zig` covers the pricing and the rate.

On 134 greedy prompts (25 each of GSM8K, IFEval, HumanEval and MMLU, 10 MGSM, a 24-prompt mix; 256 tokens, one stream), decode tok/s before and after this commit:

| | code | gsm8k | ifeval | mgsm | mix | mmlu | all |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 587 | 482 | 204 | 318 | 315 | 334 | 336 |
| after | 738 | 482 | 204 | 319 | 315 | 332 | 341 |

Every reply is unchanged. A fixed rate cannot do both: at 0.99, code reached 738 but gsm8k fell to 460 and mgsm to 303. An A/B on the same set also found the drafter's bf16 rounding (Metal parity) costs nothing: switching its conv and q/k norms to v0.6.6's rounding moved acceptance by under 0.1%.

**Verify windows and drafts.** Three more commits, on the same 134 prompts (decode tok/s; every reply unchanged at each step):

| | code | gsm8k | ifeval | mgsm | mix | mmlu | all | ms a round |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| after the copy pricing | 738 | 482 | 204 | 319 | 315 | 332 | 341 | |
| sm_120 verifies 32 rows on one weight pass | 793 | 486 | 206 | 313 | 312 | 339 | 343 | 16.49 |
| a DFlash2 hold grows its whole tree | 810 | 520 | 209 | 318 | 321 | 352 | 354 | 16.51 |
| `tf_q35_rope(8)`: a block a row and head | 816 | 524 | 210 | 320 | 322 | 354 | 356 | 16.42 |

- A window past 16 rows ran as 16-row tiles that each read the weights again (16 rows 13.4 ms, 32 rows 22.3 ms on the 27B). `Affine4Kernels.wide_verify` (set on GB10 as before, and now by the Qwen3.5 engine on sm_120) sends 17 to 32 rows to the existing 32-row verify kernel: 17.8 ms. On the 5090 its one-row results are bit-equal to the split-K decode's on all 18 contract shapes. A 64-row tile measured no gain; wide windows are compute-bound here.
- A lone stream asks the drafter for depth 1 while a context copy is ahead, and for less near a reply's end, so those rounds verified a one- to six-node tree beside the copy. The drafter's pass costs the same at any depth, so a hold now grows its whole tree whenever drafts are asked, and allocation still picks the rows. On sampled replies (temperature 0.7, fixed seeds) the 134 prompts went from 302 to 308 tok/s. Doing it in the depth rule instead captured less and cost code (771).
- `tf_q35_rope(8)` took a block a row and rotated the heads in turn; it now takes a block a row and head (query heads, then key heads) with one head staged. Each value's arithmetic is the same.

**Sampled rounds.** Each sampled row of a window launched `tf_draw` on one 1024-thread block in turn, about 97 us apiece: 1.5 ms of a 16-row round, so sampled rounds cost 17.6 ms where greedy ones cost 16.2. `tf_draw_rows` draws a run of rows in one launch, row r under its own rule and position, with the arithmetic a one-row `tf_draw` does, so every token is unchanged (a kernel set built before it keeps the per-row launches). On the community-v1 benchmark (`tensorfold benchmark`, managed server, five repeats), with all 24 replies byte-identical:

| tok/s | code, T=1 | chat, T=1 | code, T=0 | chat, T=0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 361.4 | 203.4 | 340.6 | 256.2 |
| after | 390.6 | 222.4 | 340.5 | 256.1 |

**Attention keys.** A warp of `tf_q35_attn_partial(8)` walked its chunk one key at a time (the key's load, its warp sum, then the value's load), so a 128-key chunk was bound by load latency. The keys' rows and values now load eight at a time and their dots reduce together; the running max, sum and output still take each key in turn with the same operations, so every value is unchanged. A round drops from 16.24 to 15.85 ms with bf16 rows (four keys at a time: 15.95, sixteen: 15.91), and on the 134 prompts with e4m3 rows from 16.49 to 16.03 ms (all 353 to 362 tok/s, code 795 to 805); every reply is identical. Community-v1: 400.6 / 229.2 / 350.8 / 264.0 tok/s (code T=1, chat T=1, code T=0, chat T=0).

**Lane planner: which context copies keep the 0.94 prior.** Every copy appended past a lone stream's drafts was priced from `cfg.copy_rate`'s 0.94, a prior worth sixteen rows that a stream's one or two copies never moved, so windows kept growing past 16 rows for copies that did not land. Traced over the 134 prompts: a copy after a context match of 20 or more tokens landed 85% of its rows (code's), one copied out of the prompt in the reply's first 64 tokens 89% on code (restating the asked-for function), and the rest 0 to 13%; outside code, rows past the 16th landed 11 of 777 priced. Those two kinds keep the prior; the others start from 0.08 with a history of their own, which trusted copies teach too. The proposer reports where its last match's continuation starts (`Proposer.lastEnd`). Three runs each, every reply unchanged: code 810 / 819 / 813 before and 803 / 817 / 813 after, gsm8k 525 to 533-534, mgsm 331-332 to 335, mmlu 354 to 357; rounds 16.06 to 15.92-15.95 ms. A unit test in `windows.zig` covers the rule and the two histories.

**Drafter vocabulary.** The drafter's logits came from the whole 248,320-row head, 450 us a round, where DFlash2's vocabulary (the Metal drafter's and the qwen27 engine's) is the head's first 98,304 rows and its last 288: 182 us. Drafting only those spans costs multilingual replies, whose tokens sit between them (MGSM 332 to 230 tok/s), so a stream drafts over the spans until its prompt or reply holds a token outside them, then over the whole head; a lane hold now carries the stream's tokens (`lanes.drafter.Hold.tokens`). On the 134 prompts all 364 to 367 tok/s (code 813-817 to 831, MGSM 335 kept), a round 15.92 to 15.73 ms; every reply unchanged.

**Sliced top-k draws.** `tf_draw_rows` took each sampled row on one 1024-thread block passing over the vocabulary several times (195 us a round). Both of `gpu_sample`'s candidate paths reach the row's top_k by value then id, which its tail sums and races, so for a top_k up to 32 each 8192-entry slice takes its own top_k (`tf_draw_slice_top`) and a block a row sorts them and runs the same tail (`tf_draw_rows_finish`, in `sample_slices.cuh`). Sampled replies are byte-identical (the community-v1 fixtures and the 134 prompts at temperature 0.7); a sampled round drops from 15.59 to 15.39 ms. Community-v1 now: 414-415 / 233 / 358 / 263 tok/s.

**Slot scan.** A tree window's delta-rule scan reduced each value row's k . state sum and then its output with their own `warp_sum` (four butterflies a step for two rows) and kept its slots in registers that every step copied through. As the qwen27 engine's `tf_gdn::tree_kernel` does, a step's sums and the previous step's outputs now reduce in one `spread_sum` (the same lane pairs as `warp_sum`, so every sum is unchanged), each output written a step later, and the slots are the warp's rows of shared memory. Every reply is identical; a round drops from 15.43-15.49 to 15.29-15.35 ms on the community-v1 fixtures, and the 134 prompts go from 367 to 369 tok/s (code 832 to 841).

**Row kernels.** `tf_q35_tap` took a row on one 256-thread block of scalar loads (9.3 us a launch) and `tf_q35_mlp_act` one entry a thread (2.0 us, 70 a round); both now move eight entries a thread through 16-byte loads (`qwen35_rows.cuh`), each entry's arithmetic and the activation's in-order group sums unchanged: a round 0.06 ms quicker.

**Sampled drafts follow the draw's noise.** A sampled round accepts a draft when the target's Gumbel race (keyed by the stream's seed, the position and the token) picks it, but the drafts ranked candidates by the drafter's logits alone. As the qwen27 engine's `draft_tree.best_first` does, a sampled hold now scores each candidate at the stream's temperature plus 0.7 times that draw's noise (`lanes.gpu_rule.uniform24`), and a lane hold carries the stream's sampling (`lanes.drafter.Hold.sampling`). Replies are unchanged. Over 20 seeds of the community-v1 fixtures at temperature 1, tokens a round go from 6.244 to 6.573 on code and 3.716 to 3.951 on chat (the qwen27 engine: 6.481 and 3.902; weights 0.35 and 1.0 measured lower). Community-v1 now: 428-430 / 249 / 361-362 / 265-266 tok/s.

**A one-window verify round skips `tf_q35_conv_commit`.** For a recorded window of two rows or more, `gdn_pre` logs every row's conv tail and the commit returns at once, yet each of the 48 linear layers launched it; a lone stream's rounds no longer do. The activation also takes four entries a thread (twice the blocks). Every reply identical; a round 0.1 ms quicker, the 134 prompts 371 to 372 tok/s. Community-v1: 431-432 / 250-251 / 363-364 / 267 tok/s.

Checks: `zig build test`, `test-kernel-contract`, `test-golden`, `fuzz-cortheon`, the Flash Next gate test, `zig fmt` and the lean check pass, as do the `test-qwen35-*` host steps (the draft frame host test now expects the drafter attention's 128-thread chunks, the verify host test covers sm_120's 32-row windows, and the draft equality test bounds a grown tree by its node budget instead of the asked depth).

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: a shared round's greedy streams draft their MTP heads together
items.body:
Depends on #1069 (drafted windows of several streams verified in one pass; this uses its lanes with row spans). The branch carries #1069's two commits (`3ced86d9`, `71fc0971`) under its own one (`5cc536ce`), so only the last commit is this change; I'll rebase once #1069 lands.

## What this changes

The recipe's "Not yet" list says the MTP head drafts one stream at a time. With #1069 the verify windows of a round
share one pass, but the head still ran each stream's absorb pass and chain steps alone: on a GB10 at four streams a
round spent ~29 ms in head passes, against ~5 ms at one stream (per-pass timing: a verify pass is ~42 ms + 2.6 ms a
row, the c=4 chat round 110 ms).

- `facts()` sets `.draft_streams`, so the lanes core asks a shared round's drafts in one call (as Nemotron's and GLM's
  backends do).
- `draftBatched` takes the call's greedy streams (no trees, no media): rollbacks as before, then `Ops.draftMany`: each
  stream's kept rows absorbed in one head pass (`forwardHeadMany`, a lane each on its own head cache and position),
  then one pass a chain step for the streams still drafting, every active stream's best read in one download. Each
  stream picks and stops by the same rule as alone (confidence, count, chain limit).
- Every row of a batched head pass runs the ops a lone `forwardHead` runs on it (row-wise kernels, the per-lane
  attention of #1069), so each stream gets exactly the drafts it gets alone.
- Sampled streams, trees and media keep the one-at-a-time path. `TF_FLASHNEXT_BATCH_HEADS=0` restores it for every
  stream; `TF_FLASHNEXT_DEPTH_LOG=1` prints each stream's chain length by round width every 200 calls.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `main` `d1018b31` + #1069 + this branch; one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0);
  `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local@b9ce18a6`, `TF_FLASHNEXT_DRAFT_HEAD=affine4`, `--parallel 4 --context 40960`.
  The numbers below were taken on a local stack that also carries #1143 and #1147 (prompt-side, no effect on decode).
- Exactness: with the batched head and with `TF_FLASHNEXT_BATCH_HEADS=0` every request's rounds and accepted/drafted
  counts are equal (four-stream chat: 100 rounds, 155/256 each; code: 56 rounds, 199/229), i.e. the same drafts;
  `bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial`: concurrent == alone 4/4, drafted == `"draft": false` 1/1.
- Decode speed (`bench_concurrent.py`, 256 tokens, greedy, aggregate tok/s):

  | | one at a time | batched | |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | 4 streams, code | 130.2 | 150.7 | 1.16x |
  | 4 streams, chat | 88.9 | 99.8 | 1.12x |
  | 1 stream, code / chat | 70.7 / 44.2 | 70.7 / 44.3 | 1.00x |

  The four-stream chat round falls from ~110 to ~98 ms.
- Chain lengths at four streams (`TF_FLASHNEXT_DEPTH_LOG`, length: stream-rounds): 0:3 1:229 2:60 3:157 4:43 5:100
  6:144.
- Kernel contract: no kernel changes.
- Tests run: `zig build test --summary all` (built `-Dnvcc`): 211/211 steps, 2,959 of 2,973 tests passed, 14 skipped.
- Not run, and why: sampled streams (they keep the one-at-a-time path); two ranks.

## Gotchas

- **Stacked on #1069:** the diff against `main` includes its commits until it merges.
- **Greedy streams only:** sampled streams, trees and media still draft one at a time, so their speed is unchanged.
- **Local stack:** the numbers were taken on a stack that also carries #1143 and #1147. Those are prompt-side, but this branch alone wasn't timed separately.
- **Chat still trails vLLM MTP3 at four streams:** 99.8 against 104.8 tok/s. Code is ahead, at 150.7 against 108.6.
- **Not run:** two ranks.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false` (8/8), concurrent equals solo (8/8), and a resumed two-turn prompt equals a fresh one (7,147 of 7,184 tokens restored), each equal to `main`'s output (MTP drafts on, `--prompt-cache-gib 4`; measured at `5cc536ce`, before the later lean fix, which only folds comments and moves code). Each stream gets the same drafts as alone.
- [x] No precision traded for speed. The bits do not change.
- [x] No GPU kernel changes, so the kernel contract is unaffected.
- [x] Prompt processing is unaffected (decode-only change).
- [x] Platforms: CUDA on GB10 (sm_121), one rank. No Metal change.
- [x] New tests: none needed beyond #1069's per-stream byte tests; the batched path is checked by equal rounds and accepted/drafted counts against `TF_FLASHNEXT_BATCH_HEADS=0`.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: the streams beside the first take KV pages from the core pool
items.body:
Branch `fn-paged-kv-pool` `336cb3f7`. It is #1156's `ce5b78d7`, then #1169 (`85aeb4bf`, the same change as `f23b5ab5`), then this change. It uses #1156's
`served()` and host plan.

## What this changes

`TF_FLASHNEXT_KV_PAGES=n` is off by default; n must be a multiple of 4. One stream keeps its own caches. Every other
stream takes a pool lane (`cuda_kv_lanes.zig`), which holds only its page table while idle:

- Its attention caches are n-position pages of one arena, enough for its prompt, its reply and a drafted window. With
  the MTP head a page holds the head's cache too, as the layer after the model's.
- Its DeltaNet states, convolution and n-gram tails and the head's buffers (window streams, scores, saved rows, spare
  states; `Draft.initIn`) are one run of consecutive pool pages, claimed when the stream opens (`Pool.claimRun`) and
  given back when it closes. Only addresses move.

The host plans the pool from `Loaded.layout` (fixed: the table and image rows; pages a token; the run) and admits through
`fits`. A request waits (`LaneMemory`) when no lane, pages or run is free. A lane's pages and run go back once the
engine's stream drains. Prompt-cache copies of the head's cache follow its pages. The layout is made after the head is
loaded, so the run covers every buffer the head maps (`initIn` refuses a short run).

`TF_FLASHNEXT_KV_PAGES_ALL=1` puts every stream on pages, for checks. Two ranks, `--slide` and a captured set refuse
the variable.

## Receipt

- At n=256, `--parallel 4 --context 40960`, MTP: "3 more taking 594 pages of 256 rows (4.36 GiB) as they need them,
  0 MiB fixed each". Before the run change each lane held 369 MiB from load (states, head cache and buffers).
- With MTP drafts:
  - concurrent == alone 4/4 and serial 1/1, outputs equal to contiguous;
  - drafted == plain 8/8, concurrent == solo 8/8, resumed == fresh (7,147 tokens), all equal to contiguous.
- Pages only (`--parallel 5`, 4 lanes, 792 pages, 8 requests, some waiting): the same bytes, and a kept state with its
  head cache restored into a lane.
- Without drafts, with the states in runs: see Gotchas (within noise of contiguous, bytes equal).
- Tests: full `zig build test -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc` exit 0 (the admission test sets the new field), fmt
  clean, lean 0 new findings; `kernel-contract` 85/85, 7 controls red.

## Gotchas

- **Stacked on #1156 and on #1169:** the diff against `main` includes #1156's qwen commits up to `ce5b78d7`, and the page-table change, until those land. Only the last commit is this change.
- **Off by default** (`TF_FLASHNEXT_KV_PAGES`). Two ranks, `--slide` and captured sets refuse it.
- **No-drafts speed with the states in runs:** within noise of contiguous. These are two rounds of fresh server starts on this tree, with replies byte-identical to contiguous (code/chat tok/s):
  - c=1: contiguous 23.44/23.13 and 23.71/23.73; pool on 23.57/23.55 and 23.55/23.55; pages only 23.60/23.50 and 23.64/23.48.
  - c=4: contiguous 64.7/64.7 and 66.0/64.9; pool on 65.4/64.9 and 66.0/65.5; pages only 65.8/65.3 and 65.0/64.2.
- **Waits:** in pages-only mode with more requests than lanes, a waiting request can wait several seconds (up to 9.5 s seen with 8 requests on 4 lanes).

- [x] Drafted == plain, resumed == fresh, concurrent == solo, as measured above.
- [x] No precision traded for speed. The bits do not change.
- [x] New and changed kernels are registered with the kernel contract, with red controls.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: attention caches readable through a page table
items.body:
Branch `fn-paged-kv` `f23b5ab5` on `main` `d1018b31`. Part of #781's follow-ups (other families on the core pool).

## What this changes

The seven `flashnext_attn.cu` kernels that touch a stream's caches now take a `Pg` argument: an int page table, the
elements in a page, and the positions in a page. They are `fn_attn_prep(_media)`, `fn_qsa_pool(_media)`,
`fn_qsa_scores` and `fn_attn_chunks(_ahead)`. `pg_at()` finds each row:

- with no table, it is the old expression;
- with a table, it is the start of the page that holds the position, plus the row inside that page.

A page of n positions holds, for each attention layer:

- the keys, values and indexer keys of its n positions;
- the pooled rows of their n / 4 blocks.

A cache pointer is its layer's part of page 0 (layout in `cuda_pages.zig`). Only addresses change; no sum changes
order. So paged caches give the contiguous bytes at any page size that holds whole blocks.

- `TF_FLASHNEXT_KV_PAGE_TEST=n` reads each stream's caches through a reversed table of n-position pages. It is for
  checks only.
- `fn_attn_chunks` looks up a key's row once per tile (`key_at` in shared memory, beside `key_ids`), and the pool kernel
  once per block of four; the contiguous path pays one uniform branch.
- Prompt-cache saves and restores copy page runs in the contiguous layout, so kept states move between the two forms.
- A captured Triton set refuses a page table.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `main` `d1018b31` plus this branch; one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0, nvcc 13.0.88);
  `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local@b9ce18a6`.
- Kernel contract: `tf-cuda-test flashnext-pages`, also run inside `kernel-contract`.
  - Six cases: cached lengths up to 9,000; pages of 16, 48, 128, 256 and 512 positions; two streams shuffled through
    one arena.
  - Paged output equals contiguous over three repeats for: queries, indexer queries, block scores, dense and sparse
    attention rows, the stores, and the pooled rows.
  - Attention rows stay within a float64 bound, and the guards are intact.
  - Controls are red: a swapped table over placed pages, and a planted row.
  - Gate 5: new nvcc 13.0 records for the five kernels whose register counts moved. All seven pass live. The 13.2
    override set still needs regenerating with nvcc 13.2, which is not on this box.
- Served, greedy, `--parallel 4 --context 40960 --no-drafts`, ABAB against `main` (c=1 tok/s code/chat, TTFT):

  | arm | replies | c=1 | ~8k | 31k |
  | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | main, run 1 / 2 | - | 23.46/23.40, 23.38/23.48 | 6.04-7.00 s | 25.67 / 26.01 s |
  | this, contiguous, run 1 / 2 | equal (3 chats, three ~8k, one 31k) | 23.51/23.49, 23.55/23.44 | 5.97-6.91 s | 25.64 / 25.74 s |
  | this, page test 16 | equal | 23.56/23.38 | 6.05-6.90 s | 26.08 s |

  The page test's first version (one page-table lookup per 16-byte load) cost +3-4 % at 31k; one lookup per key per tile
  removes that.
- Gates with MTP drafts, page test 16, compared with contiguous:
  - drafted == plain: 8/8;
  - concurrent == solo: 8/8;
  - resumed == fresh: yes, with 7,147 tokens restored into pages;
  - every output equals contiguous.
- Tests: full `zig build test -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc` exit 0, `zig fmt --check` clean, lean check 0 new
  findings; `kernel-contract`: 85/85 kernels pass gates 1-4, 7 controls red (exit 1 only from `main`'s 877 limit

- **Gate-5 records:** the nvcc 13.2 override set for the five kernels whose registers moved isn't regenerated, because there is no nvcc 13.2 here. The 13.0 records are new.

items.title: cuda qmmf: half tiles for decode calls whose 64-column grid leaves SMs idle
items.body:
## What this changes

A 16-row MXFP8 or BF16 lane call (decode rows, verify windows) whose 64-column grid holds fewer than 96 blocks
(`TF_QMMF_HALF_BELOW`, 0 for never) takes a 32-column tile: half a packed 64-column tile's n8 tiles, which are
contiguous in both formats' word order and in MXFP8's scale order. Each column's mma chain, its K slices and the
cluster sum are the 64-column tile's, so its bits are the same; the grid has twice the blocks. The existing instances'
loads stay behind `if constexpr (BN == 64)`.

On Flash Next's ModelOpt checkpoint the hyper-connection down projection (`[324, 10240]` BF16: 6 column tiles x 8
K slices, one block an SM on a GB10) read its weights at 158 GB/s.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `main` `d1018b31` plus this branch; one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0, nvcc 13.0.88);
  `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local@b9ce18a6`.
- Exactness: `tf-cuda-test lane-half`: MXFP8 and BF16, fp32 and bf16 out, bytes equal to the 64-column tile at Flash
  Next's decode shapes (hyper-connection down with and without its 4 inject rows, the router, the shared expert's
  gate/up and down), 1 to 16 rows, the 32- and 96-column edges; fp32 outputs within their float64 bound (worst 0.011).
  Served, greedy, against `main`: chats and ~8k contexts byte-identical.
- Kernel time on weights read from DRAM (copies past the L2, cycled):

  | call | 64-column | half | |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | BF16 1 x 324 x 10240 (hc down) | 42.0 us | 36.3 us | 0.86x |
  | BF16 1 x 320 x 10240 | 35.8 us | 32.9 us | 0.92x |
  | BF16 1 x 512 x 2560 (router) | 16.7 us | 16.1 us | 0.96x |
  | MXFP8 1 x 640 x 2560 (shared gate/up) | 12.9 us | 12.3 us | 0.95x |
  | MXFP8 1 x 2560 x 640 (shared down) | 11.1 us | 10.3 us | 0.93x |

  Wider grids gain nothing (0.97-1.02x at 160 to 320 blocks), hence the threshold.
- Decode speed (served, `--no-drafts`, one stream, code / chat): 23.95 / 23.83 tok/s, `main` 23.58 / 23.66; four
  streams 65.9 / 65.5 aggregate, `main` 65.6 / 65.1.
- Prompt speed: unchanged (prompt rows take the 64-row tiles).
- Kernel contract, `tf-cuda-test kernel-contract` (built `-Dnvcc`) on the GB10: `SUMMARY 87 kernels: 87 pass gates 1-4,
  0 fail, 0 known findings; 8 controls: 8 red as planted, 0 missed; 1533 limit problems` (the limit problems are the
  offline audit's on this nvcc, the same count as a main-based run; none in the new launches).

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: the hyper-connection normalize over 256-column slices
items.body:
## What this changes

`fn_hc_normalize` ran one block a (row, stream): at a decode row four blocks of 256 threads scaled 10,240 values while
thread 0 of each summed the stream's ten square-sum partials. `fn_hc_normalize_cols` takes a block a (row, stream,
256-column slice); every block sums the same partials in the same order (`__fadd_rn`, then the same IEEE division and
square root), so every value's bits are `fn_hc_normalize`'s, with forty blocks a decode row. `hcNormalize` takes it
whenever the width is a multiple of 256 (Flash Next's 2,560); `fn_hc_normalize` stays as the contract's baseline.

A second commit does the same for `fn_hc_dense_mix`, one 32-thread block a (row, 32-column group): `fn_hc_dense_mix8`
runs eight groups a 256-thread block, a warp each, with the same per-value ops and the same in-order group sum, so
its bytes are `fn_hc_dense_mix`'s.

Flash Next's decode spends 9.9 ms a token in its hyper-connections (per-op-class cudaEvent timing), of which the
normalize was 0.82 ms (96 calls of ~8.5 us); the rest is the two BF16 projections and three more row kernels.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: no zero fills the one-rank ModelOpt pass reads back unchanged
items.body:
## What this changes

Two fills a layer that a one-rank pass over ModelOpt weights (`nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local`, local-inference-lab's
NVFP4 exports) never needed, found with per-op-class timing of the batched pass:

- The MoE output `y` (`[rows, 11, dims]` fp32) was cleared before the experts. The down kernel writes every routed
  slot and `sharedScatter` the shared one, so at one rank nothing reads a cleared value. A rank that skips the shared
  slot (tensor parallel) still clears it.

  stays NaN), so every output bit is the same. The zero slice is filled when the scratch is allocated; a legacy lane
  that writes slices into `part`, or a native one past `cap` rows, marks it spent and the old path runs. Kept branches

items.title: lanes: prompt steps for the 27B and behind --drafter, and a share of wall time for prompt work
items.body:
## What this changes

A long cold prompt on the native CUDA engine stops every other stream. Two causes, three commits.

1. **`3aa8718d` (lanes.drafted).** The drafter's wrapper offered the lane host no `prefill_step`. Behind `--drafter`, every family's prompt therefore ran whole at admission, even where the target steps its prompts. Over a target with `prefill_step`, reported fill and `features`, the wrapper now steps too: it runs the target's step, then gives the drafter that step's rows (all but the prompt's last, as the streamed prefill does).
2. **`bd64eb6d` (qwen CUDA).** The Qwen3.5 family ran a whole prompt pass inside `prefill`. `prefill_step` now runs the same pass one cut a call: the same `nextCut` boundaries, forwards and marks, in the same order. The pass reports its fill, and a cancel lands between cuts.
3. **`34560aa8` (lane host).** The host alternated one prompt step with one decode round. `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_SHARE=p` in (0, 1] gives prompt steps a share p of wall time while streams decode:
   - a step that took t owes the decoders t (1 - p) / p of rounds;
   - a prompt with at most 512 rows left never waits;
   - only the order of whole steps changes, never a cut;
   - p = 1, the default, is today's alternation.

**Stacking.** On `main` @ `f8d254c5e` (it contains chaog992's lone-driver halt fix, `010850d74`). Branch `prefill-interleave`.

## Receipt

- **Environment.** One GB10 (sm_121), CUDA 13.0, Zig 0.17.0.
  - 27B: Qwen3.8-27B MLX 4-bit.
  - Flash Next: `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` @ `b9ce18a6`, served from a symlink folder with a rewritten index (see #1187).
  - `--parallel 4`, no prompt cache, `--no-drafts` unless noted.
- **The test.** Stream A is decoding a long reply. 5 s in, B sends a cold prompt; 0.5 s later, C sends a 34-token chat. Measured: B's and C's first token, A's longest pause, and A's rate while B fills.

**Baseline (`main`).**

| | B prompt | B first token | C first token | A longest pause | A during B (before) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 27B | 35,139 | 157.2 s | 156.9 s | 157.4 s | 0 tok/s (13.9) |
| 27B | 97,709 | 1,352 s | 1,351.7 s | 1,352 s | 0 (14.0) |
| Flash Next (1,536-row steps) | 35,140 | 27.3 s (25.6 alone) | 1.06 s | 1.30 s | 1.0 (22.8) |
| Flash Next | 97,715 | 77.2 s | 1.56 s | 1.82 s | 0.9 (23.6) |

The 27B stops everyone for the whole prompt. Flash Next already steps, but its decoders get one token per 1.1 s step: 4 % of their rate for the whole prefill.

**This PR.**

| | p | B first token | C first token | A longest pause | A during B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 27B, 35k | 1 | 179.0 s (+14 %) | 0.34 s | 1.39 s | 1.5 tok/s |
| 27B, 35k | 0.5 | 323.9 s (2.06x) | 0.19 s | 1.39 s | 6.9 (49 % of 14.0) |
| Flash Next, 35k | 0.5 | 51.6 s (2.0x alone) | 0.96 s | 1.26 s | 10.9 (50 % of 21.8) |
| Flash Next, 35k | 0.75 | 35.0 s (1.37x) | 0.95 s | 1.25 s | 5.7 (26 %) |

Predictions written before each run:
- Every result after the change landed in its predicted range.
- The 27B baseline missed high. I predicted 15-45 s at 35k and 450-900 s at 98k; main's 128-row prompt chunks run at about 224 tokens a second at 35k, and slower further in.

- **Exactness.** Token hashes against `main`'s plain run (1 stream, no drafts, no cache):
  - 27B with stepped prompts, p = 1 and 0.5, 4 streams with the prompt cache, run twice (resumed at 4,736 and 2,816 tokens): 48 of 48.
  - 27B with the DFlash2 drafter through the stepped wrapper, p = 0.5: 24 of 24.
  - Flash Next at p = 0.5 with MTP drafts, 4 streams and the prompt cache, twice (resumed at 4,854 and 2,864): 24 of 24.
- **Tests.**
  - A new host test (`drafted_step_test.zig`) runs a stepping target's prompts through the wrapper three steps at a time; the replies equal the whole prefill's.
  - The fake target now holds a cold stepped pass's rows as each step makes them.
  - Full `zig build test -Dnvcc=…`: 276/276 steps, 3454/3469 passed, 15 skipped (missing libjpeg/libwebp and hardware), exit 0.
  - lean_check: 0 new. fmt clean.
- **Contract.** No new kernel.

## Not run, and why

- Metal: no Mac. Metal's Flash Next steps since 1.1.2 (#1032), and the share applies to any stepping family behind the lane host.
- A decoder's pause below one step: it is still one whole step (1.25 s for Flash Next's 1,536 rows, up to 1.4 s for one 27B cut). Going lower needs smaller steps on each family's own cut grid.

## Gotchas and overlap

- #1080 (BobClawblaw, 4096-row chunks for the 27B) and #1078 (cancels between chunks) change the same prompt loop in `families/qwen3_5/cuda_native.zig`. `bd64eb6d` is a thin split of that loop: whichever lands first, the other rebases. With 4096-row chunks, a 27B step becomes the whole wait a decoder sees (about 4 s).
- #1120 (drama3: bounded prompt rounds with fixed cuts) follows the same pattern for another family.

## Questions for @ashhart

1. **The default p.** It is 1 today: the old alternation, so no default behaviour changes. p = 0.5 halves both sides; 0.75 keeps decoders at about a quarter while the long prompt is 1.37x slower. Do you want a default other than 1, chosen by family or by measured cost?

items.title: flint: serve Recursive Flint (40B-A2.5B MoE) natively on Metal
items.body:
Serves Recursive's Flint (`RecursiveSI/flint`, a 40B-A2.5B MoE) natively on Metal from Recursive's MLX INT4 export, by the lane host with the prompt cache, structured output, tools and several streams. Closes #1175.

## What changes

- **`moe_route` (core, first commit):** `tf_route_logits` gave each lane four 32-wide slices of k, which covers a hidden width of exactly 4096; at Flint's 2048 it read past each row and past the packed router. Each lane now takes `hidden / 1024` slices (still four at 4096, so GLM-5.3-Flash's and Step-5's routers keep their arithmetic), `source` refuses other widths, and `round_logits` rounds each logit to bf16 as a bf16 router matmul gives it.
- **`families/flint` (second commit):** config and weights (U8-stored affine words, bf16 norms and sinks); 35 sliding (513-token window, RoPE) and 14 full (NoPE) GQA layers with per-head q/k norms and a learned sink a head; two dense SwiGLU layers, then 256 routed experts (top 6 by sigmoid score, renormalized) beside an ungated shared expert. Rounding follows MLX's points as RecursiveSI's `rec_mlx` computes the model (bf16 residual, `rms_norm` as `w * bf16(x * inv)`, SiLU op by op, bf16 router logits).
  - Attention: prompt chunks on the tensor units (gemma4's prompt kernel over a position-major cache, the sink in the denominator); decode rows on `sdpa_vector`'s lanes over key blocks at absolute positions, merged with the sink as MLX's second pass does, so a row's bits do not depend on the rows beside it. Sliding layers keep a ring of the window plus one prompt chunk.
  - q|k|v and each MLP's gate|up are stacked into one matrix at load (one launch, the same row sums; about 270 MB of copies); one launch norms and rotates q and k and writes k and v; residual adds are fused with the next norm.
  - Routing uses core `moe_route`'s logits, then a top-k pick a simdgroup a row (the core select's arithmetic without its per-Mac lists).
  - Several streams' windows share one forward; a lone stream's steps run a step ahead (`gpu_tokens`), drawn on the GPU (argmax, or the keyed sampler of lanes' `gpu_rule` / `gpu_full`, Nemotron's kernels at Flint's vocabulary) into a token ring, and host draws use the same sampler's twin.
  - `tf-flint-run`: greedy tokens, every position's logits, forced steps, step timing, and `exact` (one-row steps against windows of any width, bit for bit); `docs/recipes/flint.md` and a README row.

## Checks (Apple M5 Ultra, 256 GB, macOS 27; `RecursiveSI/flint-int4` at 3b93f9053b530488405ae9fca51d4900d6ce21f0; this branch's head)

**Against the reference** (RecursiveSI's `rec_mlx` model on MLX 0.32.4 with plain bf16 KV caches; its own server quantizes the full layers' KV, so it is not the reference here):
- Greedy, a 13-token chat prompt: 64 of 64 tokens equal.
- Teacher-forced along the reference's own greedy continuation, 48 steps after each prompt (native: prompt in chunks, then one row a step):

| 2,628 tokens | 0.0030 | 0.0337 | 46/48 | step 13: reference 17098 over 2847 by 0.016, native 2847 by 0.039; step 38: reference 12917 over 20479 by 0.047, native 20479 by 0.422 |

- For scale: the reference's own prompt pass and its one-token-at-a-time pass disagree on 3 of 13 rows of the short prompt (KL up to 7.0), at the same near-ties the native decode path takes.

**Window exactness** (`tf-flint-run exact`: the reference's continuation as one-row steps and as windows after the prompt, every row's bf16 logits compared): 0 of 48 rows differ at 2,628, 6,426 and 31,597 tokens with 16-row windows, and at 31,597 with windows of 1, 2, 5 and 11. A turn resumed from the cache starts in 0.068 s against 0.726 s cold. Not compared against `rec_mlx`'s server or `mlx_lm` (neither serves this model with an unquantized KV cache).

**Memory:** 21.4 GiB of weights wired; caches 28 KiB a token in the full layers (7 GiB a stream at 262,144) plus the sliding rings; weights, scratch and caches stay under 75% of RAM or `FLINT_LOAD_LIMIT_GB`.

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1: the FP32 and FP64 oracles run side by side
items.body:
Piece (e) of the #690 split, stacked locally on piece (d) (#827): the FP32 and FP64 oracles share one equation set, and a new `oracle-precision` mode runs both widths on identical checkpoint bytes and the same tokens.

The form of the sensitivity gate is the open question in #847/#827. The gate-deciding number is the whole-model NRMS between the FP32 source contract and the FP64 ideal on the *same* checkpoint with the GPU out of the loop: if it is small, FP32-level arithmetic is not where the residual gaps come from; if it is large, arithmetic is the bound. This mode makes that measurement reproducible in one invocation instead of argued from separate receipts.

**What changed**

- The reference modules (`math`, `projection`, `engram_math`, `reference`, `attention_math`) take a comptime real width. The FP32 contract and the FP64 ideal are the same equations with `Real = f32` or `f64`, so the two paths cannot drift apart: every sum, reciprocal root and rounded store is one expression instantiated twice.
- `tf-dsv41-run oracle-precision MODEL TABLES IDS_JSON OUT_DIR` runs the teacher oracle at both widths over the same bytes and tokens (window capped at 16 IDs, one teacher step), keeps `reference-fp32-logits.f32` and `reference-fp64-logits.f64`, and reports `normalized_rms_error` (against the FP64 logits), `normalized_rms_error_against_fp32`, `max_absolute_error`, `rms_error`, per-token argmax, both wall times and `evidence_origin`.
- The mode captures its residency counters before it prints the per-token argmax and writes the artifacts, so the gate measures execution rather than the invocation's own diagnostic I/O.
- `math.zig`'s FP64 narrowing now tests the FP64 class and returns the canonical quiet NaN of the input's sign. Before the repair the payload branch looked only at `bits >> 49`, so every positive FP64 NaN became a finite BF16 word - `0x3ff8` for the smallest signalling NaN (`0x7ff0_0000_0000_0001`), `0x3ffc` for a quiet NaN - and negative NaNs kept non-canonical payloads (`0xffff` for the all-payload NaN).
- New reference tests cover every FP64 IEEE class through the narrowing (both infinities, both zeros, the largest finite overflow, FP64 subnormals, and six NaN payload classes), the BF16 subnormal and overflow tie grid against the FP32 branch, and the frozen FP32 outputs of projection preparation/rotation/output, the hyperconnection stages, attention pooling and the Engram gather. The frozen words were captured at `53b790082`, before the repair; the repair touches only the FP64 narrowing, so those FP32 words must not move.
- `docs/deepseek-v41.md`: the mode, the command and its window.
- A host test pins the mode's arity, beside the one that pins the lane arguments.

**Receipt**

Environment: commit `964183651`, the 2.9bpw pack (the repack the #827 receipts qualified), 8 teacher token IDs, one Apple M3 Ultra (80-core GPU, 512 GB unified memory), macOS 26.6.2, Zig 0.17.0. Tests on `964183651`: `zig build test-deepseek-v41-reference` 43/43 steps and 32/32 tests (the compiled test binary prints `All 32 tests passed.`); the full `zig build test test-golden` suite result is recorded in the follow-up section below; `tools/zig/lean_check.py` reports 501 problems on this tree against 501 on the parent commit, 0 new; `zig fmt --check zig` clean. ### Review follow-up (round 2)

The review asked for three things; this commit (`964183651`) is the response.

1. **`math.zig:30` no longer narrows a positive FP64 NaN to a finite BF16 word.** The old line tested `magnitude > 0x7ff0_0000_0000_0000` and rebuilt the word from `bits >> 49`, so `0x7ff0_0000_0000_0001` became the finite `0x3ff8`, `0x7ff8_0000_0000_0000` became the finite `0x3ffc`, and the negative all-payload NaN became `0xffff` instead of `0xffc0`. 2. **Class/edge tests and frozen old-versus-new FP32 outputs.** The class table covers positive and negative signalling/quiet/all-payload NaNs, both infinities, both zeros, the largest finite FP64 value that overflows, and the smallest/largest FP64 subnormals; the tie table covers 16 BF16 subnormal/overflow ties plus the 7 neighbouring parity values. The frozen tests span projection (`prepare`, rotation and output narrowing), the hyperconnection folded/expanded and pooled boundaries, attention pooling and sparse-head selection, and the Engram gather. They assert exact `u16` words, so a change in FP32 arithmetic fails them rather than passing inside a tolerance.
3. **Raw arrays, IDs, pins and logs.** The invocation wrote `reference-fp32-logits.f32` (4,136,960 bytes, sha256 `9698a8aaf3640869fc69fe539819845519cb1c0f94c72a5d5dedc1a94ced93ab`), `reference-fp64-logits.f64` (8,273,920 bytes, sha256 `696de82fca773faa8329e4efca66e3caff4fc1d62c0d5d8ae596aee69176a037`), `precision-fp32-vs-fp64.json` (sha256 `0f34cc96ee47781504ee10473b18369eb4b36f0e956720e2dabd023244576143`), `residency.json` (sha256 `6cc7717fe5735f8bfa69223bda5c1188686163a3bc35c521af114c84d51095a3`) and the run log (sha256 `2a8d8eb823ad8c1fd042689373faa9a0ec7e777ece2915d3dc8cdb98dd97f303`). The two logit arrays are byte-identical to the arrays produced before the repair on `53b790082` (same two sha256 values), which is the same evidence as the frozen FP32 tests: the repair moved only the FP64 NaN path. The 8 tokens' argmax are `5, 41079, 294, 270, 344, 11111, 16, 660` at both widths, 0 greedy disagreements.

Full `zig build test test-golden --summary all` (cold cache outside the worktree): `Build Summary: 311/311 steps succeeded; 4442/4457 tests passed (15 skipped)`, exit 0. The log's `failed command:` lines are expected negative-path output from tests that simulate backend failures; every build step succeeded.

Checklist: every token still goes through the lane rounds and no serial path is added — this is an offline diagnostic mode, so the drafted/resumed/concurrent legs are unchanged from (d). No precision is traded: the mode measures precision, it does not gate it. No new or changed GPU kernel. New tests skip cleanly without their dependency (the reference harness runs weight-free); on the pre-repair sources the NaN and frozen-word tests fail, and in this PR's first revision the modules did not exist at all.

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash: read the weights once per decode window
items.body:
## What this changes

GLM-5.3-Flash's decode windows (MTP verify rounds of 2 to 16 rows) read each weight once per window in `glm_rows`, instead of once per pair of rows. Every row keeps its single-row bits.

- `tf_rp_rows_at` takes three rows in one pass, holding their inputs as bf16, and runs four or more rows as pairs inside each 512-input chunk. Each row's sums keep the single-row order.
- `glm_rows` runs threes, pairs and a last row. `glm_rows_wide`, for windows of four or more rows, runs eights and a four first, so its registers stay out of the 1- to 3-row kernel.
- Each simdgroup takes 2 columns instead of 4, so the 4,096-output projections (KDA and MLA out) run twice as many simdgroups.
- `glm_rows_gather`, which runs prompt chunks' routed experts on the wide formats, takes the same pairs path at four rows, with the same sums. On iQ-MLX-5.1bpw, whose prompt chunks take that path, cold prompts of 2,048 to 65,536 tokens take 26% less time.
- `glm_rows` and `glm_rows_gather` reserve the 64 threads a group they launch. Xcode's M1 and M2 builds of these kernels change with the requested thread count in no monotonic order, so the offline limit search returned 0 for them, including for `glm_gather`'s existing records. The `glm_rows` launches are registered with the kernel contract's limits gate.

Overlaps #1066 and #1114 in `wide.zig`'s pipeline count and the `glm_gather` records in `registry.zig`; whichever lands second needs a small rebase.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `d1018b31` (main) and `4c5f79b2` (this PR), each built with `zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1` (Zig 0.17.0, Xcode 27.1). items.title: Flash Next CUDA: drafted windows of several streams verified in one pass
items.body:
## What this changes

Draft, as agreed: the MTP verify windows batched across streams in the lanes engine, with the same bit-for-bit contract. Is the "CUDA per-stream drafting precision" work on #286 touching `cuda_mtp_ops.zig` / `verifyFn` too? If so, I'll rebase this onto it rather than collide.

`verifyFn` ran one batched pass per drafting stream, so a round over N streams read the weights N times and the aggregate stayed flat (81.8, 70.3 and 64.0 tok/s at 1, 2 and 4 streams on a GB10, code prompt, `--parallel 4`). Now the drafted windows of a round share one pass, up to the round's 64 rows (`TF_FLASHNEXT_WINDOW_ROWS`, 0 keeps each window alone; never past `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK`).

- `batch.Lane` gains a row span and the lane's own rollback (`keep`), hidden-row (`streams`) and score (`logits`) destinations. `rows = 1` and none of them is the one-row round as before, which keeps its launches. A lane's `keep` may hold a window's DeltaNet rollback only (`rollbackOnly`); a training pass's kept tensors are refused, as the round already refuses `moe_add`.
- Per lane, with the row count and launches its lone pass makes: n-gram gather, media inject, PLE convolution and tail, DeltaNet front, chain (to the lane's kept state) and conv shift, attention (rope, cache writes, pooling, indexer scores, selection, chunks).
- Once over all rows: the matmuls, hyper-connection blocks, router, experts and head. An untaught stream's rows read no pocket, as in `round`.
- `Engine.windows` (`cuda_prompt_windows.zig`) runs the pass. `Ops.verifyMany` refuses every window before any stream's state moves, then leaves each stream as its `verify` leaves it (saved tail and PLE rows, host scores row, `fed`). `verifyFn` groups the drafted windows (`cuda_lanes_verify.zig`). Plain one-row rounds and two ranks keep their paths (two ranks would need one wire command for the batch).

2 commits, 16 files, +376/-48, all in `zig/src/families/flashnext/` (`cuda_batch*.zig`, `cuda_prompt*.zig`, `cuda_mtp_ops.zig`, `cuda_lanes*.zig`, `cuda_round_graph.zig`, which refuses a window it never captures, `cuda_media.zig` and two test row types) and `zig/tests/cuda/` (`flashnext_windows_tests.zig`, `main.zig`).

With every lane reading the first lane's position it fails (`124152 of 124160 words differ`).

- Aggregate tok/s, 512 tokens each, same binary with `TF_FLASHNEXT_WINDOW_ROWS=0` (each window alone, main's path) and the default:

  | prompt | T | 1 stream, alone / shared | 4 streams, alone | 4 streams, shared | |

  | code | 0 | 80.9 / 80.5 | 79.9 | 134.0 | x1.68 |

items.title: Living Weights on Qwen3.8 Flash Next (CUDA, GB10): the pocket in every pass, the trainer, and --slide
items.body:
## Stack

This sits on two open PRs, so it opens as a draft until they land:

- #869 (Flash Next on CUDA) and the backward kernels PR on it (`lw-c-fnback`, 4 commits on #869's head 7746bb9d);
- #878 (Living Weights as a core module, `lw-b-core` 75978a1c).

The branch is `lw-c-fnback` plus one merge commit of `lw-b-core` (46627a81), then the 4 commits below (the fourth is docs). That merge is
the only one: the trainer needs the CUDA family from #869 and the learner in `zig/src/living` from #878, and neither
contains the other. It touched `zig/build/cuda.zig` (both modules kept) and `native/cuda.zig` (the host keeps
`@hasDecl(F, "slide")` until Flash Next declares one). Once #869 and #878 land, I will rebase this onto `main` and the
merge goes away; the diff to review now is `lw-c-fnback...lw-d-fnlearn` after the merge, or the 4 commits.

## What this changes

1. **A taught folder's pocket in every pass** (03767e5d). #869 refused a folder whose shared experts carry Living
   Weights neurons. Now the engine packs each shared expert's own 640 rows as before and keeps the pocket's neurons in
   fp32 (`cuda_pocket.zig`); every pass (prompt chunks, drafted windows, decode rounds) adds them behind the shared gate
   on the layers that have any, through #787's two-kernel form ported to this family (`tf_fn_pocket_in`, then `_out`;
   a layer with no neuron launches nothing). On such a layer the MoE output is summed in fp32 in MODE 2's order
   (`fn_moe_sum`), the pocket added, and written back rounded once (the write-back's one-slice MODE 4). Every other
   layer writes back exactly as before, so an untaught folder's bits do not change (receipt below). The pocket's
   kernels are row by row, so drafted equals `"draft": false` and concurrent equals solo with a pocket too.
   The batched pass can also keep what a backward reads: each read-out's input streams, normed rows, v, up rows and
   inject gates, the mixer's and the MoE's branches, the MoE's input and slots, attention's projections and gated rows,
   the final mixer's read-out. The up rows come from `fn_hc_upmix_up`, our read-out kernel writing the rows its mix
   reads (the same mixed bits as `fn_hc_upmix`). A captured comparison set's `_qmm_upmix` keeps none, so `--slide`
   refuses a captured set.
   #869's config check refused a taught folder's wider shared expert, which the first restart in the receipt below
   found: `cuda_config.zig` now takes the width with the pocket's neurons (`tensorfold_learned_neurons`, a whole number
   of groups, 128 at most), with a test.
2. **The trainer** (6db9e3e8). `cuda_train.zig` runs the learner's passes (keys, loss, target) with sequences side by
   side on the engine's own batched pass: `cuda_batch_train.zig` runs the row-wise launches over every row, and the
   n-gram block, DeltaNet and attention one sequence at a time from position 0 and zeros. The open fact's neurons are
   scaled per sequence, and each nudge joins its layer's MoE output. The loss's gradient then runs from the 4-bit head
   down to the lowest nudged layer with `flashnext.fn_back` and `cuda.gdn_train`, reading the engine's packed experts
   where they sit and MLX copies of the small linears (`cuda_train_buf.zig`). Both files are under 600 lines (the old
   676-line trainer is split in two). `zig build flashnext-learn` checks it on the GPU (receipt below).
3. **`--slide` for qwen4_exp on CUDA** (0986c5a5). `living/families.zig` lists `qwen4_exp`: a SwiGLU shared expert at
   every layer behind its own gate, 4-bit groups of 32, keys under `text_config`, the MTP layer's expert in the index.
   This replaces #878's stand-in test family, whose tests now read the real entry. `flashnext/living.zig` gives the
   layout and writes the pocket through the core's shard writer (`pocket_shards_test.zig`: the first save widens every
   expert, the MTP head's with zeros, and tells `text_config`; a later save lands in place; every other byte kept).
   `cuda_slide.zig` hosts the core learner over the trainer, and the lane backend opens with `--slide`: the trainer's
   1,024 rows in the pass's scratch, the layout from config.json, and the trainer's bytes kept out of the streams' room.
   The native host's existing rules still apply (`--slide` on a GB10 only, no `--segments`, a folder of links refused).
   Macs keep refusing `--slide` for this model.
4. **Docs** (47748f75): the Flash Next CUDA recipe and the Living Weights page (what a GB10 needs for Flash Next, and
   this receipt as measured), and a CHANGELOG line.

## Receipt

- Environment: `lw-d-fnlearn` 47748f75 (this PR's 4 commits on the merge 46627a81 of `lw-b-core` 75978a1c into
  `lw-c-fnback` a5d183d5, itself on #869's 7746bb9d), Zig 0.17.0; NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121), driver 580.178.04,
  CUDA 13.0.88, Ubuntu 24.04.5; checkpoint `leimroth-lab/Unbound-LR7` revision 2ae3a2ff (Qwen3.8 Flash Next, MLX affine
  4-bit group 32, MTP head). "Probes" below are 23 greedy chat requests of up to 120 tokens: 12 questions about the
  user (two or three wordings for each fact taught below) and 11 unrelated prompts (capitals, arithmetic, a haiku, a
  Python one-liner and so on).
- **An untaught folder serves as before.** #869's head and this branch's head on the same snapshot: the 23 probes give
  the same replies, drafted (23/23) and with `"draft": false` (23/23). Decode speed (`tools/bench_openai.py`, 256
  tokens, median of 3): drafted 83.9 and 62.3 tok/s on code and chat against #869's 84.1 and 62.6; `--no-drafts` 35.1
  and 35.1 against 35.0 and 34.9. A cold 3,001- and 12,001-token prompt (`tools/bench_cache.py --require-cold`, time to the first token): 2.66 and 10.27 s
  against #869's 2.71 and 10.28 s. The model takes 75.82 GiB against #869's 75.81.
- **The trainer's forward is the serving forward.** `zig build flashnext-learn` on the snapshot (one prompt of the
  Python engine's reference set, its first 256 tokens, the last 32 the answer):
  - a row's scores never depend on later rows (the last token changed, every earlier row's scores byte for byte, at 255
    and 254 rows);
  - the trainer's keys pass and loss pass over 119 rows against the serving forward (`Engine.forward`, every row's
    scores): every layer's MoE input and shared gate and every row's scores byte for byte, untaught and with a pocket
    neuron at layer 31;
  - six sequences side by side give each one's loss exactly as alone (672 rows, 0 difference);
  - a pocket neuron moves the forward by exactly gate act v at its row (1.503 against 1.503).
- **The gradient against finite differences.** In bf16 a finite difference is noisy: below about a bf16 ulp of the
  residual the rounding decides, above it the loss's curvature does. The check nudges each layer's MoE output at the
  last row (its nudge reaches only its own loss: the direct path) and at a row before the answer (it reaches the loss
  only through later rows' attention and DeltaNet: the cross-row paths), at layers 12, 23, 31 and 42, along the push and
  half along a random direction, in four windows of the prompt (offsets 0 to 3), with least-squares slopes over
  steps of plus and minus one to six times 0.4% and 3% of the residual's size (32 checks a path and a step). Over all
  four windows the direct path's median relative error is 10.6% at the small steps and 111% at the large ones; the
  cross-row paths' is 43% at the small steps and 16% at the large ones (worst 204% and 69%). The first window's last
  row disagrees at every layer (2% to 73% at the small steps, about 2x at the large ones); in the other three windows
  the direct path agrees with a median of 6.2% at the small steps (worst 25%, 71% in one check of 8, and 17%), and
  the last row of the same prompt's first 255 tokens agreed within 0.3% to 11% at layers 12, 23, 42 and 46. So the
  direct path holds where a finite difference can see it, and the cross-row paths stay noisy, as they were with the
  captured kernels before #869's own. The kernels themselves are each checked against
  float64 in the previous PR.
- **Lessons.** A fresh copy of the snapshot (the files a lesson rewrites copied, the rest hard-linked), served with
  `--slide --context 8192 --no-thinking --temperature 0`, taught these five facts one learn request each (`"source":
  "chat"`), with the probes after each lesson:

  | fact | kept | rounds and steps | seconds | its probes right after | after all five |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | "My name is Zack." | yes | 2 rounds, 2 steps | 571 | 3/3 | 0/3 |
  | "I used to live in [a US city]." (city left out here) | yes | 2 rounds, 2 steps | 524 | 3/3 | 3/3 |
  | "My GitHub name is ZackSample." | yes | 2 rounds, 2 steps | 631 | 1/2 | 1/2 |
  | "I contribute to TensorFold." | no: "too few clean answers to learn from" (one clean question) | none | 14 | 0/2 | 0/2 |
  | "I have two DGX Sparks at home." | no: the held-out answers did not come back | 5 steps over several rounds | 2,389 | 0/2 | 0/2 |

  None of the 12 probe wordings was among the 85 questions the lessons trained on, so every probe is held out: 4 of 12
  after the five lessons. The first fact came back on all three wordings after its lesson and on one after the
  second lesson, none after the third. After the second lesson that is #870 (a refit silences the earlier fact). After
  the third it is the corrections rule: the server took "My GitHub name is ZackSample." as replacing "My name is Zack."
  and retired the name fact's neurons (the graph says `replaced by fact 3`), because both answer a "what is my ... name"
  question. This PR uses #878's learner as it is; with #876/#877 applied the name fact survives the second lesson (see
  the comment below), and the false replacement is a separate lesson-writer fix. The 11
  unrelated prompts kept the untaught model's replies byte for byte. A kept lesson took 8.7 to 10.5 minutes: 2.5 to
  4.1 writing the lesson, 2.9 to 4.1 the trainer's first round (one step), then 0.6 to 2.1 for the second round and
  about 25 s of checks a round.
- **A taught folder serves.** The copy after the five lessons (27 neurons in its pockets) restarted without `--slide`
  and with it: the 23 probes give the same replies as the teaching server did after the last lesson (23/23 each).
  Drafted equals `"draft": false` (23/23), and four streams at once (`--parallel 4`) equal each alone (23/23). A
  1,670-token prompt asked again resumes 1,663 tokens from the prompt cache and gives the fresh reply, drafted and
  with `"draft": false`. Decode:
  drafted 79.8 and 59.1 tok/s on code and chat (5% below untaught), `--no-drafts` 34.7 and 34.5 (1% below). Cold
  prompts: 2.67 and 10.30 s for 3,001 and 12,001 tokens.
- **Memory.** The server reports the model at 75.82 GiB and 10.59 GiB kept for the trainer (its buffers take
  10.23 GiB: MLX copies of the small linears it reads, the keep lists for 1,024 rows, the backward's scratch);
  `flashnext-learn` holds 84.24 GiB of device memory with the engine and the trainer, 84.59 GiB at its peak. During a
  lesson the GB10's 121 GiB showed 92 GiB in use.
- Tests: `zig build test-cuda-host` from a fresh cache: 33/33 steps, 546/546 tests pass; `zig build test-living`: 39/39
  (#878: 38, the one more is Flash Next's shard writer test). Every commit after the merge builds (`zig build`, `native`,
  `test-cuda-host`, `test-living`) and passes `zig fmt --check build.zig zig`; `python3 tools/zig/lean_check.py` gives
  527 problems against 527 on `main` (0 new); all 46 fatbins build for sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121 and `check_fatbins`
  passes. On the head build, `tf-cuda-test` `flashnext-hc` (its read-out kernel now also has the form that keeps the up
  rows), `flashnext-attn`, `route-rows`, `norm-rows`, `experts-rows`, `fn-back` and `fn-pocket` all pass.
- Not run: Metal (Macs refuse `--slide` for this model as before; whether a Mac serves a folder taught here is not
  checked), sm_86 and sm_120 cards.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo.
- [x] No precision traded for speed. If the bits change, the description says which sums change and why. (Untaught:
  no bits change. Taught: a layer with a pocket rounds its MoE output once after the pocket is added in fp32.)
- [x] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release. (Untaught, same speed as #869; see the receipt.)
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran, Metal M1 to M5 and CUDA, and which I could not. (GB10 only.)
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency.
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

## Not in this PR, said plainly

- The learner's own fixes found on Flash Next: the forgetting bug (#870), lesson-writer fixes and the re-check of earlier
  facts. This PR runs #878's learner as it is, and the receipt shows what that gives.
- Faster lessons: the lesson writer and the trainer's first round take most of a lesson's time; neither is tuned here.
- The MTP head's shared expert is widened with zero neurons on a save and served without a pocket, so drafts are made
  without the learned facts; verify windows run the main model's pockets, so drafted replies still equal undrafted ones.
- The DeltaNet backward's projections dequantize per sequence (see the previous PR).
- `flashnext-prompt`'s row-by-row reference path (#476's check tool) does not add a pocket; only the batched pass serves.
- The gradient's cross-row paths are not confirmed by finite differences (above).

## Questions

- `Trainer.scores` (a loss pass that stops at the scores) exists for `flashnext-learn`'s byte check against the
  serving forward. Is a check-only method on the trainer acceptable, or should the check live behind a build option?
- Should `qwen4_exp` live in `living/families.zig` (as here), or in the family folder (`flashnext/living.zig` already
  holds its layout and writer), as asked on #878?

items.title: Living Weights on Qwen3.8-27B (CUDA, GB10): the pocket in every pass, the trainer, --slide, and pocket neurons that no longer drive one another
items.body:
## Stack

This sits on two open PRs, so it opens as a draft until they land:

- #726 (BobClawblaw: #608, philip-pentatonic's Qwen3.8-27B CUDA engine, brought to 1.0.11 with image input, an fp8 KV
  cache and a prompt cache). #608 alone sits on 1.0.5, while the learner below sits on `main`; #726 is #608 on a base
  the learner merges into (and the base this port was built and measured on), so this stacks on #726, not #608.
  #608's commit (99bcc5b2) keeps philip's authorship; nothing of it is rewritten.
- #878 (Living Weights as a core module, `lw-b-core` 75978a1c).

The branch is `pr726` (bcd433c0) plus one merge commit of `lw-b-core` (dac84b63), then 3 commits. That merge is the only
one: the 27B's trainer needs #608/#726's qwen27 CUDA family and the learner in `zig/src/living` from #878, and neither
contains the other. Its conflicts were `zig/build/cuda.zig` (the qwen27 and living modules both kept, qwen27 imports
living) and `native/cuda.zig` (#878's slide adapter behind #726's `@hasDecl(F, "slide")`). Once #726 and #878 land I
will rebase onto `main` and the merge goes away; the diff to review is `dac84b63..lw-27b-pr`.

The first of the 3 commits carries learner work that is also open as its own PRs (the refit and recheck fixes for #870,
facts learned in conversation), as this port runs it; it shrinks to the 27B-specific parts when those land.

## What this changes

1. **The learner as the 27B's lessons run it** (e90a1035): on #878's `zig/src/living` and the server's lesson code:
   - #870's refit and recheck fixes and the conversation fix, as in their own PRs;
   - checks score a reply asked before through serving's own decode rounds instead of decoding it again
     (`slide_known.zig`, the learner's `score` request), and the lesson writer's asks run side by side;
   - **the drift fix** (below): `pocket_decouple.zig`, `Trainer.pocket_back`, broad keep prompts and drift checks;
   - `families.zig` lists `qwen3_5` (a dense SwiGLU MLP at every layer, ungated, 4-bit groups of 64);
   - `pocket.zig`, `learner.zig` and the server's big files split to stay under 600 lines.
2. **Core training kernels** (b9b3e835): the Gated DeltaNet layer's forward for training and input gradient
   (`gdn_train.cu`, `cuda/gdn_train.zig`; the same bits as serving's chain at `--fmad=false`) and gated attention's
   backward (`attn_train.cu`), family-neutral. `tf-cuda-test gdn-back`, `gdn-back-27b`.
3. **The 27B learns** (018d2b2a):
   - `qwen27/cuda/pocket.zig`: fp32 SwiGLU pocket neurons beside every MLP, added after the down projection in every
     pass (prompt chunks, drafted windows, decode rounds), row by row, so drafted equals `"draft": false`; an untaught
     stream (the lesson writer's judge) reads no pocket. A taught folder's widened MLP keeps its own 17408 rows tiled.
   - the trainer (`train.zig`, `train_more.zig`, `train_load.zig`, `train_ops.zig`, `qwen27_train.cu`): keys, loss and
     target passes with 16 sequences side by side on the engine's own batched pass; the loss gradient from the
     group-64 head through the dense MLPs and pocket, attention and the DeltaNet on MLX copies of layers 12-63
     (18.9 GiB); wide 4-bit products and a backward over only the rows a nudge needs (same bits); pocket input fits on
     the GPU with the host's bits; greedy scoring through decode rounds (a prompt pass over prompt + reply is not
     decode's arithmetic on this model: 0/576 rows bit-equal, 4/576 argmaxes differ at near ties).
   - `tap.zig`: a prompt in a conversation read through the engine's prompt pass (the context fix's `tapRows`).
   - `--slide` for `qwen3_5` (`slide.zig`, `native.zig`); the pocket written through the core's shard writer.
   - `tf-qwen27-learn`: packed passes against one at a time, the push against finite differences, `Q27_GATE` (gate
     taps with activations), `Q27_SCORE` (replies teacher-forced through serial decode); `tf-cuda-test q27-back`,
     `q27-gemm`.

## The drift fix

On a 21-fact scale test (below) the taught model's unrelated replies drifted as facts accumulated, and some grew
garbage tokens (`$x` -> `$xdera`, `Waves` -> `WavesToggleButton`). Gate taps on every unrelated reply row found why:

- On the untaught model's states the learned neurons barely leak (of 160 neurons x 3,435 unrelated rows: 0.06% above
  zero, at most +0.56). With the pocket live: 113 of 160 neurons reach above 0.25 somewhere, up to u.x = +16.5 (the fit
  targets about 1). At each garbage row about 100 of the 160 fire at once, layer by layer: one fact's neuron leaks
  +0.43 on a digit in LaTeX, its own next neurons read +0.8, +5.3, +16.2, then other facts' neurons follow.
- The same cascade runs on the facts' own questions: at a probe's decide row, untaught states give the fact's own
  neurons a median +0.94 and no other fact's neuron above 1 (0/6,400); live, 662/6,400 other facts' neurons read above
  1 (one probe: 77 of them, up to +30). The lesson logs show it growing: earlier facts' neurons firing on a new fact's
  questions read at most 3-7 by lessons 6-8 and 10-33 from lesson 13, and their refits fail. This is why later facts
  got harder to learn, not a neuron budget (at most 9 of a layer's 64 neurons were used).
- Cause: a neuron at layer L reads x = s * h / rms(h), so a lower pocket neuron's output v moves its product by
  (s * u) . v. The values fit backpropagated through the higher neurons' activations ((u x)^2, unbounded) and learned
  outputs that drive them; later lessons stacked on that.

Fix: every output is kept off what the neurons above its layer read (s * u, s from the trainer's optional `readScale`),
every input and refit off what the neurons below write there (s * v), and the values backward holds the pocket's
activations (`pocket_back`). Projecting a finished folder's outputs this way removes the cascade at once (other facts'
neurons above 1: 662 -> 25 of 6,400) but loses recall, since its outputs were fitted with the chains; fitted under the
constraint from the first lesson, recall holds (receipt). Two cheaper guards come with it: 92 broad keep prompts
(other languages and scripts, math and LaTeX, code, verse, lists) read as rows a fact stays silent on, and 12 drift
checks whose replies a round may not change where the open lesson's own neurons read above zero (a reply tipped at a

## Known limits

- The cascade is cut on the residual stream's direct path; an injected fact can still reach other facts' detectors
  through the model's own layers (seen as other facts' neurons rising from -0.5 to +1.5 behind a leak), so a leaking
  neuron on a row no lesson read can still change a reply. The broad keep prompts and drift checks narrow that.
- Each output is kept off up to (neurons above) directions in 5,120: a few hundred facts' worth before that space
  binds.
- The first commit duplicates the open refit/recheck/context PRs until they land.
- The CUDA kernels were checked on sm_121 only.
